story:
The pasta was still steaming when Alexandra's phone buzzed against the water glass, and she read the message twice before she let herself look up. "We have a problem," Branden had written. "West Council passed their version. Eleven to four. Ours passed ours on Monday. They're not the same." Her father was saying something about the diurnal rhythm of his new shift schedule, days collapsing into nights, and she nodded at him while her thumb typed a reply under the table.

"What's urgent enough to ignore my riveting account of sleep deprivation?" her mother asked. She taught twelfth-grade government at the school across town, and she had a way of asking questions that were already answerable.

"The book-locker bill," Alexandra said. "The two student councils were supposed to pass the same rule. Free periods, no locked shared lockers, something like that. But West cut out the appeals process we wrote in, and they added a fine. Monday is the deadline, and the principal won't sign off on two versions of one rule." She turned her fork in the sauce without eating. "Branden thinks we should just push our version through again and dare them."

Her mother demurred, tilting her hand as if weighing something invisible. "And what happened when Congress tried that?" It was her mother's habit to answer questions with questions, which used to infuriate Alexandra and now mostly trained her. Alexandra started to say that Congress had nothing to do with lockers, and then stopped, because the analogy was already assembling itself somewhere behind her eyes.

"Wait," she said. Branden, who wanted their version to win outright, believed the answer was force. Adriel, who had texted earlier, believed the answer was surrender, drop the bill, try again next year. Alexandra had been holding both messages in her head like two hands pulling the same rope. But there was a third thing, something from her mother's classroom, from the posters she'd stared at during conferences. "When the House and the Senate pass different versions of a bill," she said slowly, watching her mother's face for confirmation, "a conference committee of members from both chambers writes a compromise."

"Which both chambers then have to pass," her mother said, and went back to her plate.

Alexandra was already calling Branden. The connection crackled in the quiet kitchen, and his voice came through half-swallowed by hallway noise, a leitmotif of locker doors slamming behind him. "We can't make them take our version," she said. "We pick people from each council, sit down with West's people tonight, write one compromise, and then both councils have to vote on it. That's the whole mechanism. It's not winning. It's not losing. It's the only thing that gets the bill to the principal as one rule instead of two."

"West will never agree by Monday," Branden said, but she could hear him turning it over, the way his voice dropped when he stopped arguing and started thinking. "Who picks the committee?"

"You, me, and one more from ours. Three from theirs. And I think Adriel should be our third." There was a silence on the line long enough for Alexandra to notice her father had stopped pretending to eat and was watching her the way he watched weather coming in. Adriel had wanted to drop the bill. Adriel would walk into that room already convinced compromise meant defeat, and Alexandra wanted him there anyway, because a compromise built only by people who already agreed was just her version wearing a borrowed coat.

"Fine," Branden said. "Library at seven. If West shows up."

They showed up, all three of them, arms crossed in the corner carrel where the light was worst, and for the first twenty minutes it went exactly as badly as Alexandra had privately feared. The West delegate, a senior with a lanyard and no patience, kept sliding their fine back across the table like a stone he was unwilling to lose. Adriel sat with his chin in his hand, unhelpful on purpose. It was Branden, of all people, who leaned forward and said, "Take the fine out and we'll give up the appeals board. Written warning first, then the principal." Adriel lifted his head.

Alexandra wrote the sentence down, word by word, and read it aloud. Around midnight, both councils voted by message, and the counts crawled in one by one on her cracked screen while she sat very still at the cleared dinner table. Hers passed first. Then West's tally filled in, and she read the last name on the list, and pushed her chair back from the table.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
story:
The laminated sheet appeared on the pool door on Tuesday, taped at eye level where the usual schedule hung, and by Wednesday morning half the team had decided it was a punishment. Daniel read it while waiting for the chlorine smell to stop being the first thing he noticed every morning, which it never did. Fifteen minutes of on-deck work before anyone touched the water: single-leg balances, hop-and-stick landings, cutting drills between cones. Below the list, in smaller print, a sentence about neuromuscular warm-up programs that train balance, landing and cutting technique reducing the risk of knee ligament injuries.

Katrina slapped the sheet with the back of her hand. "Fifteen minutes. Do you know what I could do with fifteen minutes? Sleep. Eat a croissant. Live my life."

"We're in the water for two hours anyway," Daniel said. "What's fifteen more?"

"That's not the point. The point is the principle." She externalized everything, Katrina did, every small grievance dragged out into daylight and given a name, and the team loved her for it, mostly.

Ms. Wijaya, who coached the water polo squad and had apparently taped the sheet, said only that the routine started Thursday and the first match was Saturday, so there would be exactly two sessions to get it right before it counted. Then she went into her office and closed the door, which everyone agreed was suspicious. Coaches who believed in something usually lectured you about it until your ears bled.

Thursday, Sara-Maude balanced on one leg at the edge of the deep end like a heron with a grudge, arms out, wobbling. "This is dignity," she announced to the echoey room. "This is what dignity looks like. Take a photo for my mother."

"Hop and stick," Daniel called, reading off the sheet he'd borrowed from the door, because someone had to keep track and he'd been volunteered by not objecting fast enough. "Two hops forward, land soft, hold it."

"Why soft?"

The honest answer was that he didn't know, so he said, "Because the sheet says so," and Sara-Maude hopped, landed with a sound like a dropped melon, and swore at the ceiling. Behind her, Katrina did the cutting drill, sprinting between the cones with sudden changes of direction, and afterward stood with her hands on her knees breathing hard. "Okay," she admitted. "That one's actually terrible in a useful way. My legs feel like lawsuits."

Daniel had his own theory forming, and it was not yet a good one. His theory was that Ms. Wijaya had simply found a new way to fill the dead time before the pool opened, that the routine was busywork with a scientific varnish, and that the small print on the sheet was decoration. He held this theory loosely, the way you hold a suspicion about a friend, and he tested it the way you test that too, by watching for evidence.

The evidence arrived Friday at the second session, in the person of the trainer, a wiry woman who came in with a bag of cones and stayed to watch Katrina do the cutting drill. "Knees tracking over your toes," she said. "Good. When you planted that last one, you were a centimeter from caving inward." Katrina, who could not let a statement pass without commentary, said, "And if it caves inward, what happens, exactly?" The trainer shrugged. "Ask your knee ligament. Actually, don't. You'll want it intact."

That night Daniel typed the small print into his phone, word for word, and the sentence came back at him from a dozen places, the same claim in every one: neuromuscular warm-up programs that train balance, landing and cutting technique have been shown to reduce the risk of knee ligament injuries. He sat on his bed in the blue light and felt the two theories grind against each other, busywork and prevention, and he noticed something slightly embarrassing, which was that it had never occurred to him that warm-ups were for anything other than feeling warm. You jumped in, you got loose, you played. The idea that you could rehearse the exact movements that broke people, the landing and the cutting, and get better at not being broken, seemed almost like cheating, except that it was the opposite of cheating, it was the most legitimate thing in the world.

Saturday morning the natatorium was loud, the other team shouting in the corridor, and the pool lying flat and pale under the skylights like something diurnal that had gotten up early against its will. Fifteen minutes before the whistle, Ms. Wijaya pointed at the deck. The team groaned in harmony, a practiced, musical groan, and then did it anyway, balances and hops and cuts, Sara-Maude wobbling less than Thursday, Katrina's lawsuits apparently settled out of court.

"You've converted," Katrina said, watching Daniel tape the cones down with unusual care.

"Half converted. I'm keeping the other half in reserve in case it turns out to be a scam."

"You're incapable of a full opinion. It's your tragedy."

In the third quarter a girl on the other team planted her foot to change direction and went down clutching her knee, and the pool went quiet in stages, whistle first, then shouting, then even the water seeming to hush. She was helped up and off to the bench, and the game restarted, and Daniel scored once and got beaten twice and swallowed half the pool, as usual. But between plays he kept looking at the bench, at the girl with the ice pack, and then at Katrina carving through the water with her knees tracking neatly over her toes, and he held both images without deciding what they proved, because two sessions of hopping was not a fact and one bad landing was not a statistic, and he knew enough by now to know he didn't know.

Afterward, dripping in the corridor, he found Ms. Wijaya coiling a lane rope. "So is that why you put up the sheet," he said. "The knees."

She looked at him for a second longer than necessary. "Same time Monday," she said. "Bring your own cone."

story:
Florence had pitched the table at the end of the driveway by nine, before the heat flattened everything, and by eleven the pitcher was half gone and she had made nine dollars toward the econ club's trip to the state competition. Sidney sat beside her in the folding chair, scrolling through the practice questions on a cracked phone, reading them aloud in a bored voice that made each one sound like a small insult. "Explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation," Sidney read. "Worth twenty points. We are going to lose."

"We are not going to lose," Florence said, though privately she had written and crossed out the same answer four times the night before. The difficulty was that she could recite it and did not believe it, and she suspected that the judges, like her, could hear the difference. Joaquin arrived on his bike then, freewheeling the last stretch, and put two dollars on the table without asking for lemonade, which was his way of joining the club treasury and also of stalling.

"Tell me this," Florence said. "When the central bank raises rates, why does that fix prices? I keep saying it and it sounds like magic."

Joaquin took the cup she poured him anyway. "It's not the whole answer, but there's a rule," he said. "The Taylor rule. This guy John Taylor proposed it. When inflation rises one percentage point, the central bank should raise its interest rate by more than one percentage point." He said it the way he said most things, as though handing over something he had found on the ground and did not much care about keeping.

Sidney looked up from the phone. "More than one? That's the part I got wrong on the practice set. I said match it. If prices go up one, raise the rate one. That seemed fair."

"That's what I would have said too," Florence said slowly. She was quiet for a moment, working the paper rim of her cup with her thumbnail. So the bank was not supposed to be fair. It was supposed to overshoot, deliberately, by some amount, and the whole argument of the policy lived inside that little gap between one and more than one. She thought of her mother saying you don't fight a fever by making the room exactly as warm as the fever, and then thought that her mother had never said that, that she was inventing the analogy and then crediting it, which was a habit she meant to break before college.

"Write it on the sign," Joaquin said. "People love rules."

So they did, or Florence did, in marker on the back of the cardboard price list, and the three of them argued about how to phrase it while a line of customers looked at the tennis balls and the cooler. A man from down the street, Mr. Hamdan, who coached debate at the middle school and bought lemonade every Saturday, read the sign over Florence's shoulder with his cup still raised partway to his mouth.

"Inflation up one, rate up by more than one," he read. "Whose idea?"

"John Taylor's," Sidney said. "There's a rule named after him."

"Careful with rules," Mr. Hamdan said, which was as close as he ever came to advice, and he paid his dollar and walked on. Florence watched him go and decided he meant that a rule was a starting place, not an answer, and also that she had no idea whether he meant that or something less generous.

The afternoon brought the harder question, which Sidney asked without looking up from the phone: who pays when the bank overshoots. Because somebody always pays. It was not, Florence understood, a thing that would appear on the score sheet, but once she had seen it she could not sequester it in some separate part of her mind where inconvenient questions went to wait. Raising rates by more than inflation rose meant loans that got expensive faster than paychecks grew, meant the kind of tectonic pressure that built quietly and then moved through people's mortgages and hiring decisions, meant someone like the cashier at the pharmacy where Florence's mother worked, whose hours were the first thing cut when business slowed. To stabilize prices was to lean on somebody, and the rule never said whom.

"Maybe that's why it's called a rule and not a law," Joaquin said. "It's a starting place. You still have to decide."

"That's not on the test," Sidney said.

"It should be," Florence said, and meant it, and also knew that at the competition she would write the clean version, the one with the gap between one and more than one rendered confidently in her neatest handwriting, and that she would feel a small complicity in the tidiness of it. She could hold both things now: the answer they needed and the answer she actually had, which was that the rule told you the size of the push and nothing about the people it pushed on. What she could not yet hold was whether knowing that made her better at economics or only sadder in a way that looked, from the outside, like understanding.

At five they poured the last of the pitcher into three cups and split the thirteen dollars, and Sidney counted it out twice, and Joaquin pocketed his share and said the trip was as good as funded if they sold cold brew next week. Florence copied the sign, the whole thing, rule and all, into her notebook before the ink could smear in the evening damp.

"Quinn," Sidney said, using the old nickname from middle school Spanish class, "you're going to write the sad version on Saturday, aren't you."

Florence capped the marker and looked down the street where Mr. Hamdan had gone.

"I'm going to write the true one," she said, "and then the one that scores."

story:
The line outside the middle school gymnasium was longer than Jonathan expected, and slower, so that by the time he reached the folding tables near the doors he had read every poster about provisional ballots twice. It was his first election. He had turned eighteen in March, and the registration card had arrived in the mail like a small credential, less exciting than his acceptance letters but somehow more official. Behind him, Dalton was arguing with Yousef about whether their votes mattered at all, given the district.

"Statistically, one vote decides nothing," Dalton said. "It's a ritual. We reify the ritual by showing up, like that makes it real."

"It's not a ritual for my uncle," Yousef said. He held up his phone, screen tilted so they could both see. A livestream from another country, a chamber full of representatives, a Speaker calling a division. "This is happening right now. My dad's been watching since four in the morning."

Jonathan leaned in. The numbers were climbing on a board at the front of the chamber, green votes and red votes, and a banner along the bottom of the broadcast was cycling through a phrase in translation: motion of no confidence, motion of no confidence, motion of no confidence. The count finished. The government had lost. The chamber erupted, some members standing and applauding, others slumping, and the camera cut to the prime minister, who was gathering papers without looking at anyone.

"So what happens now?" Jonathan asked. "Do they impeach him? Is there a trial?"

"That's not how it works there," Yousef said. "It's a parliament. It's not like us." But he didn't say how it did work, and the line moved, and the three of them shuffled forward past a woman with a stroller and a man still wearing his work ID on a lanyard.

Jonathan kept turning it over while he waited. He had assumed, without ever examining the assumption, that every country removed a leader roughly the way his did: a long process, an accusation, a chamber of judges, a threshold so high it had almost never been crossed. But the broadcast had shown something different, a single afternoon, a single vote, and a prime minister stacking his papers. Was the head of government just an employee of that chamber, hired and fired by it? The thought made the office seem smaller and stranger, or maybe larger, because it meant the majority in the lower house could reach up and take power back whenever it lost patience. And yet it also seemed to make the whole thing faster, almost casual. A prime minister could fall because of one bad Tuesday.

He was still holding his phone, watching the aftermath, when the anchor said it plainly, almost in passing: a government that lost such a vote in the lower house had to resign, or call a general election and put the question to the whole country. That was it. Two doors, and the fallen government itself chose which one to walk through. Jonathan read the closed caption twice. He pictured a president here losing a vote like that, and could not, and the failure of the picture told him more than any diagram in the civics textbook he had half-read senior year.

At the check-in table, Ms. Kobayashi, who had taught him world history and now apparently spent Election Day finding names in a binder, located him without looking up. "Jonathan Reyes. First time?" she said, and when he nodded, she handed him the marker to sign the line. He noticed she had a small television behind the table, muted, tuned to the same foreign channel.

"You're watching it too," he said. "The no confidence thing."

"It's called a vote of no confidence," she said, initialing his form and moving him along, already reaching for the binder again. "Third one this year over there."

In the booth, Jonathan slid his ballot out of its sleeve and looked at the names, the local ones, the ones he had researched in October and argued about with Dalton in the group chat. He found himself wondering whether any of the people on this paper, if they won, could be removed this quickly by anyone, or whether the machinery here was built the opposite way, heavy and slow on purpose, vestigial parts included, so that only the rarest crises could ever dislodge anyone. Or whether slowness just protected people nobody wanted to protect. He could argue it both ways, and he noticed that he wanted to argue it both ways, right there in the booth, with his marker hovering over the ballot.

He voted. Outside, the line had grown longer, and Yousef was holding his phone up over his head. "They're calling an election," Yousef called to him across the barrier. "Six weeks. The whole country votes again."

The card table wobbled on the second hinge, so Aiden folded a napkin into quarters and wedged it under the short leg while Avery counted the cash box for the third time that morning. Forty-one dollars and change. Avery wanted ninety by Sunday for the concert ticket, and had calculated that at a dollar a cup they needed two more good Saturdays, assuming weather held and the bike path stayed busy. Aiden's own stake was smaller, a vague promise of pizza money, but he had agreed to the whole of today's shift because Avery had a dentist appointment at eleven and because he was trying, for reasons he could not entirely codify, to be a more dependable person this summer.

The morning came on warm and slow. Sprinklers hissed across the lawns, and a man in an obsolescent walkman-era jogging suit passed twice without buying anything. At ten the radio they'd brought out on the back step, tuned to the news station because Avery's mother liked it, announced that the Federal Reserve had raised rates again to fight inflation. Aiden was pouring a cup when the customer at the table, a woman with a toddler on her hip, frowned at the radio and said, "Which rate is it they keep raising, do you know? My mortgage? Something else?"

Aiden opened his mouth and found nothing in it. He had half absorbed the phrase "the Fed raised rates" from a hundred headlines without ever asking which rates, or whose. "I think it's like the rate banks pay the government," he said, and heard the guessiness in his own voice and disliked it. The woman nodded the way people nod at weather, paid her dollar, and moved on, but the question stayed at the table with him like a wasp he couldn't leave alone.

When Meadow pedaled up at half past eleven with a backpack and an appetite for free lemonade, Aiden had his phone out and was reading with the concentration of an acolyte confronting a dense scripture. "Don't tell me you're doing homework at a lemonade stand," Meadow said, stealing a cup. "It's not homework," Aiden said. "That lady asked me a question and I made something up. Sort of. I want to actually know." Meadow leaned over his shoulder, slurping. "Know what, exactly?"

"Okay," Aiden said slowly, reading, then reading again. "So the Fed's main policy rate, the one they move when you hear 'the Fed raised rates,' is called the federal funds rate. And it's the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves." He said it out loud twice, testing the weight of it. "Not the government lending to banks. Banks lending to banks, overnight." Meadow raised an eyebrow. "Why would banks lend to each other overnight?" "I genuinely don't know yet," Aiden admitted. "But at least now I know what the thing is."

The hard part, he discovered over the next hour, was not the knowing but the saying. He tried out an explanation on Meadow, who had appointed herself a skeptical audience. His first attempt collapsed into jargon halfway through. His second was so vague it could have described anything. Meadow kept one condition on her refills: he had to make it plain enough that she, who claimed to find all economics a form of arithmetic gossip, could repeat it back. Between customers he scribbled on the inside of the poster board, crossing out sentences, hunting for the shape of the idea rather than its costume.

By two o'clock the path had thinned and the sprinklers had gone quiet. Aiden had settled, provisionally, on this: the Fed moves the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves, and that rate ripples outward until borrowing costs more everywhere, and when borrowing costs more, people and businesses spend more slowly, and prices stop climbing so fast. He could feel the seams in it, the places where he was repeating rather than understanding, the word "reserves" still slightly opaque to him. He told Meadow that too. "I can say it," he said, "but I can't defend every step of it yet. If someone asked why slowing spending tames prices, I'd probably improvise, and I saw today where improvising gets me."

At quarter to three Avery came back with a numb cheek and a revised forecast, down to one more Saturday instead of two because a neighbor had promised to buy two pitchers for a block party. While Avery recounted this, the woman from the morning reappeared on the return leg of her walk, toddler now asleep in a stroller. "You figured out that rate thing?" she asked, half smiling. Aiden wiped his hands on the towel and stood up straighter behind the table. "It's called the federal funds rate," he said. "It's the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of reserves." She looked at him for a moment, then at the radio, then back. "Huh," she said. "So what does that have to do with my grocery bill?" Aiden reached for a fresh cup, filled it slowly, and began.

story:
The practice rooms off the band hallway smelled of valve oil and old carpet, and Elizabeth had claimed the one with the working piano every Tuesday and Thursday since September. Ms. Zhou had posted the assignment on Monday: sixteen bars, a melody with chord changes, written out by hand in standard notation, due in three weeks. Elizabeth wanted it to be good, not passable, and the difference between those two things was taking up all the space in her head.

The trouble was the seventh bar. She could hear it, the melody stepping up and then holding, filling the space before it turned and came down again, but when she wrote it out the bar came up short. One beat, gone. She counted the sixteenth notes twice, tapped the pulse against the piano's closed lid, and still the bar ended a beat too early, leaving a hole where the held note should have been.

Alyvia knocked on the door with her knuckles the way they had agreed on in September, two quick and one slow. She had her theory notebook under her arm and a granola bar in her teeth. "Are you hiding or working," she said around it.

"Working. Come look at this." Elizabeth slid over on the bench. Alyvia leaned in, chewing, and read the stave with her finger hovering above it without touching the page. The radiator under the window ticked, and somewhere down the hall a trumpet worked through a scale badly, the same missed note three times.

"Your melody is right," Alyvia said. "I can hear it. But the bar's short."

"I know it's short. I don't know how to fix it without chopping the tune into pieces."

Alyvia tapped the half note in question. "What if you just make it longer?" She took the pencil from behind her own ear, and before Elizabeth could object she added a small dot after the note, then sat back on the floor with her knees up. "A dot after a note adds half the note's value. So a dotted half note lasts three beats in 4/4."

Elizabeth looked at the mark, so small on the page, so consequential. She counted it through under her breath, one-two-three, and the bar closed like a door swinging shut. "Three beats," she said. "That's exactly the hole." She played it, and the melody finally sounded the way it had sounded in her head, the held note suspending the line before it turned.

"It's funny," Alyvia said, unwrapping a second granola bar she had apparently been sitting on. "Violette got so mad about this exact thing last week. She said notation is a virulent conspiracy to make simple music complicated. She used those words. Virulent."

"She said conspiracy?"

"She was having a day." Alyvia shrugged. "I told her the symbols are just the cheapest way to get the sound out of your head and into somebody else's. She said that was too optimistic for a Tuesday."

Elizabeth copied the bar onto a fresh sheet, dot and all, then played the whole sixteen bars through. In places it worked. In the ninth bar the chord change she had chosen, a minor chord where she had first wanted major, made the melody sound sadder than she had intended, and she could not decide whether that was a discovery or a mistake. Both readings felt true. She played it twice more, once believing each one, and the music seemed to change under her hands, though the notes on the page stayed identical.

When Ms. Zhou came by during the last fifteen minutes of the period, she stood in the doorway with her arms crossed, listening without commenting. Elizabeth finished and kept her hands in her lap. She wanted to say that the piece was finished and she wanted to say that it was not finished, and both statements felt like lies from certain angles.

"The seventh bar," Ms. Zhou said. "Good solution."

"I almost didn't find it," Elizabeth said. "Alyvia showed me the dot."

"Then you'll know where to look next time." Ms. Zhou glanced at the page. "Bring the ninth bar to class on Thursday. I'm curious what you decide."

After she left, Alyvia stood and brushed cracker dust off her jeans. "What are you going to decide?"

Elizabeth played the ninth bar once, major, and once, minor. She had wanted, all along, for the assignment to be something she could control completely, every choice deliberate, arrived at by her own volition, and this was the part nobody had warned her about: that the music had wants too, or seemed to, and that following them felt less like deciding and more like negotiating. She could not prove the minor chord was better. She could only play it and feel the room tilt.

"I don't know yet," she said. "That's allowed, right?"

Alyvia zipped her notebook into her bag. "Probably. You're the one who has to hand it in."

They walked out together past the practice rooms, one of which had gone quiet, and the hallway lights hummed overhead. Elizabeth held the folder against her chest with both hands. In the ninth bar the melody went up into the minor chord and then, in the tenth, came down by step, and she caught herself walking in that rhythm, three beats and a turn, all the way to the parking lot.

story:
The thermometer read 150 exactly, and Camille pulled the roast out of the oven with a confidence she did not entirely feel. Behind her, the screen door banged twice, once for Megan and once for Hamzah, who had promised to help and had so far only helped themselves to the lemonade her mother had left in the fridge.

"Is that it?" Megan asked, peering over her shoulder at the pan. "That's the whole dinner?"

"That's the whole dinner. My parents get home at seven, and I said I'd handle it." Camille had said it in a moment of ambition, on the phone, after her mother had worked three doubles in a row and sounded tired in a new way. She had imagined herself calm at the stove, the backyard smelling of rosemary, everyone impressed. The imagining had not included the part where she stood in the kitchen alone with a slab of beef and a phone with nine percent battery.

Hamzah leaned against the counter and studied the roast like it was a problem set. "So it's done? A hundred fifty is done?"

"That's the number the recipe said. Medium well." She had the page printed out, actually printed, because her phone was dying and she distrusted herself enough to want paper. The recipe had a strange sentence near the bottom, something about resting the meat, which she'd skimmed and moved past. Now she read it again while Megan set three glasses on the picnic table on the back porch.

The sentence said the temperature would keep climbing while the roast rested.

"Keep climbing," she said out loud. "How would it keep climbing? It's out of the oven."

"Maybe they mean it stays hot," Hamzah offered.

"It says rises. It says it can rise by several degrees." She looked at the roast, glossy and brown, and felt the first thin thread of doubt. Several degrees of what, though. How many. The recipe was generous with adjectives and stingy with numbers.

Megan came back in. "Table's set. What's wrong?"

"Nothing. Maybe nothing." Camille typed carryover cooking into her phone before it could die, and the search results loaded in a slow crawl. She read with her finger on the screen. Carryover cooking, it said, means food keeps cooking after it leaves the heat, and a large roast can rise by several degrees internally while it rests. She read it twice. "So if I pulled it at 150 because I wanted 150," she said slowly, "then by the time everyone eats it, it's not 150 anymore. It's past it."

"Past it meaning what?" Megan asked.

"Meaning overcooked. Meaning dry." Camille set the phone face down on the counter as if it were suddenly an unreliable witness. The clock over the stove said 6:12. Her parents were due at seven, which was less a deadline than a wall she was walking toward. She couldn't put the roast back in to un-cook it. That was the thing about heat, she thought; it only moved in one direction, like time, which was a comparison she would have rolled her eyes at in an essay but which felt true here in the kitchen with the oven ticking as it cooled.

Hamzah, who was less a gourmand than a person who regarded food as fuel, still understood the shape of the problem. "So next time you take it out early. Like at 145, and it walks itself up to 150 sitting on the counter."

"That's the idea. Carryover cooking. But this time I didn't, so." She covered the roast loosely with foil and stood there in the yellow light of the kitchen window, listening to the cicadas start up in the backyard. Through the screen she could see the picnic table Megan had laid out, the cloth her mother only used in summer, three glasses catching the last of the sun.

"Next time," Megan said, "test it on us first. Practice roast."

Camille almost laughed. She had wanted this dinner to be a kind of proof, that she could be trusted with the household for one evening, that she was already the version of herself she kept planning to become in college. And now the centerpiece of the proof was going to come to the table slightly over the line she'd aimed for, through no carelessness of her own, or maybe exactly through a carelessness of her own, since she'd skimmed the part of the recipe that mattered. She couldn't decide which, and she found she could hold both at once, the way you can know you did your best and also know your best had a hole in it.

She carried the roast out to the picnic table while it was still too hot to carve, and set it down on a folded towel, and the three of them stood around it in the backyard with the light going amber at the edges of the fence. The tomatoes and bread were fine; the salad was actually good; the roast was the question. When her parents' car pulled into the driveway at ten to seven, she still hadn't cut into it.

Her mother came through the side gate first, still in her work shirt, and stopped at the sight of the table. "You did all this?"

"Most of it. The roast might be a little more done than I meant." Camille picked up the knife. "I took it out at the right temperature, but it turned out the temperature keeps going after the oven. It rises while it rests. Several degrees, for a big roast. I didn't know that this morning."

Her father was already pulling a chair around. "So carve it, and we'll see."

She cut the first slice, and everyone at the table leaned in to look.

story:
The wind came off the fields the way it always did in March, boreal and thin, flattening the grass inside the track oval until the white lines looked like seams on a pressed sheet. Charlie stood at the edge with a clipboard she had borrowed from her mother's office and watched the under-twelves run their scrimmage, which was what they ran every practice, every week, all season. The ball travelled in long hopeful punts. Nobody passed to anyone who wasn't already shouting for the ball. She had been put in charge because the regular coach was on leave, and because she was seventeen and had played since she was eight, and because nobody else had volunteered.

The losing was not the problem, exactly. It was the sameness of the losing. In the fourth paragraph of an article Ms. Goldberg had photocopied for her, on a Wednesday when Charlie had stayed after class to complain, she had found the idea that had been circling her all week. A 1993 study by K. Anders Ericsson and his colleagues had looked at violinists and described something they called deliberate practice: effortful work on specific weaknesses, with immediate feedback, not just logging hours. Charlie had read it twice on the bus. Then she had looked out the window at the track, where the kids she coached were logging hours, and logging them, and logging them.

She tried it out on Lyam first, because Lyam told the truth even when it was inconvenient. "So they scrimmage for ninety minutes," she said, dropping her bag on the bleacher beside his, "and they love it, and they can't complete a five-yard pass under pressure. Same as last month. Same as the month before."

"Scrimmage is fun," Lyam said, in the tone of someone defending a principle he hadn't known he held.

"Fun isn't the point. Well. Fun is a point." She showed him the photocopy, folded into quarters. "This is."

The next practice, she did not let them scrimmage. She had spent Sunday night drawing it out: a diamond of cones on the infield, two passers and one defender, the receiving player required to call the ball before it arrived. Every drill aimed at one weakness, the weakness she could finally name, which was that they passed to feet that weren't moving and to players they couldn't see. When she blew the whistle for the first water break, Sirine jogged over with her water bottle clutched in both hands, like something rescued. "Charlie, they're going to mutiny," Sirine said, not unkindly. "Joey already asked if this counts as practice or as punishment."

Charlie looked at the kids, who were standing in the boreal wind pretending to drink for longer than drinking takes. "Ask them to give it until the end," she said. "Then we scrimmage for the last fifteen minutes. Tell them I said that."

She had planned for the feedback part by making herself the feedback. She stood in the middle of the diamond and called every pass the instant it left the foot: "Good, that was early," or "Late, you waited until she was covered," her voice pitched to carry without being a shout. It was harder than she had expected. Twice she called "late" on balls that had actually been fine, and she had to enunciate her correction carefully, so they'd know she was taking it back and not just mumbling. By the third rotation she was hoarse, and Sirine, without being asked, had taken the far side of the diamond and was calling the passes there.

What surprised her was that the kids did not mutiny. They complained, the way twelve-year-olds complain about everything, in a continuous weather of grievance that meant nothing. But the small one with the lopsided ponytail, who had spent all February hiding on the wing, asked twice whether she'd gotten her call out early enough. And the passing got sharper in a way you could see, not in a way you could measure. That was the part Charlie couldn't reconcile. Her mother, an engineer, wanted numbers. Charlie had the 1993 study, and it said effortful work on specific weaknesses with immediate feedback beat logging hours, and she believed it, and she also had no way to prove that today was better than Tuesday except the look on the small one's face when the ball arrived at her feet instead of two yards behind them.

On Friday Ms. Goldberg found her at the track after practice, coat buttoned to the chin, watching the kids scrimmage under the lights. "They look different," Ms. Goldberg said.

"They pass to space now. Some of the time." Charlie pulled her sleeves down over her hands. "Half of me thinks I've figured something out and half of me thinks I've just made practice less fun for a bunch of kids who were already having fun."

"Those aren't the only halves of anything," Ms. Goldberg said, and then, because she was a person who knew when to leave, she left.

Lyam changed his mind before Charlie did, which was unusual and which she suspected she would remind him of for years. He came to watch on Thursday, sat on the bleachers with his chin on his knees, and at the end of the fifteen-minute scrimmage, when the small one with the ponytail threaded a ball through two defenders to a runner she had picked out before anyone else saw her, Lyam stood up and applauded alone, and did not appear embarrassed. "Okay," he said when Charlie climbed up beside him. "Okay. You were right and the article was right."

"I don't know if I was right," Charlie said. "That's the honest answer. It worked today. I don't know if it works because of the thing in the study or because they're twelve and they get better at everything whether I plan anything or not." She looked at her clipboard, at the cones stacked by the shed, at Sirine collecting the balls into the net bag, one by one, patiently, as though each one had had a long day. There was an asceticism in the drills she'd designed, a stripped-down plainness, and she liked it and she distrusted it at the same time, the way you can like and distrust a clean room.

"Same time next week?" Lyam said.

Charlie slid down off the bleacher rail and landed in the cold grass. "Same time," she said, and jogged out to the far end of the field, where the small one was still standing with the ball under her foot, waiting to be told what to do with it.

story:
The thermostat at his grandfather's house was set to a penurious sixty-two degrees, and Mathis sat at the kitchen table in his jacket, watching game film with his laptop angled away from the window glare. He had the footage from Saturday, the whole second half, and he had promised Coach he would text his notes to Enzo by tonight. The problem was that the notes, so far, read like an indictment. You drifted on the backcheck. You passed when you should have shot. You let their winger turn you twice. Every sentence was true, and every sentence, if he sent it, would land like a door slammed in a cold hallway.

He and Enzo had been friends since they were nine, and had been teammates for exactly as long, which was the trouble. When you know someone that well, criticism ferments into something worse than itself. Mathis let the cursor blink after "You let their winger turn you twice" and tried to imagine Enzo reading it on the bus, jaw tightening, the screen lighting his face. Last season a different captain had sent Enzo a list like this one, blunt and unadorned, and Enzo had carried it for weeks, cold on the bench, refusing to look up between shifts. Mathis did not want to be that captain. But he also could not lie and say the drifting wasn't happening, because the regional semifinal was in ten days and Enzo was the best defenseman they had.

Aryanna arrived at four to pick up the history notes she had left there on Sunday, and found him staring at the laptop like it owed him money. "You look like a man being tried for something," she said, pulling out the chair across from him. He turned the screen so she could read. She read it. "It's accurate," she said. "It's also a hostage note." She told him then about her mother, who taught eighth grade and had changed how she graded essays after reading about a study. "It was led by a guy named David Yeager, back in 2014," Aryanna said, peeling an orange with her thumbnail. "Students were way more likely to actually revise their essays when the critical comments came with a note saying the teacher had high standards and believed they could meet them. My mom started writing one sentence on top of every paper. High standards, and I know you can hit them. Revision rates went up."

Mathis said the obvious cynical thing, that it sounded like a trick, a compliment stapled to a wound, and Aryanna said it wasn't a compliment, it was a belief, which was different, and anyway Enzo would know the difference because Enzo knew him. She finished the orange and put the peels in the bowl his grandfather kept for exactly this purpose, since the compost was across a yard he refused to cross in slippers.

He thought about it while she copied the history notes by hand, because her phone was dead and his grandfather's printer had not worked since the previous administration. He thought about his grandfather's poker club, actually, a little polity of six old men who insulted each other with total freedom and total love, and who had kept the club going for forty years. Mathis had once asked him how they did it, and his grandfather had said, "Because everybody knows everybody else thinks they can play." That had seemed like a non-answer at the time. Sitting at the cold kitchen table, it did not.

So he deleted nothing and softened nothing. He kept "You let their winger turn you twice" and added, above the whole list, one line, and it took him four tries to make it not sound like a greeting card: I'm sending this because you're the best defenseman we have and I think we can win the semifinal if you play like it. Then, uncertain still whether it was honesty or a tactic, he sent it before he could revise the sentence a fifth time, and closed the laptop, and helped Aryanna find the second history folder, and ate the orange sections she left on the table for him.

His phone buzzed twenty minutes later. Winger twice, huh. Then, before Mathis had decided whether his stomach was dread or something else: Fair. Send me the clip at 1:15, I want to see my feet. And then a third message, which was just the video call request, and Enzo on the tiny screen in the dark kitchen saying, "Okay, run it back to the faceoff and watch my left skate, I think I'm cheating toward the boards."

story:
The gym smelled of rubber and cold metal, and Aidan was missing his fifth shot in a row when Mr. Menon blew the whistle and pulled him aside. That was the deal for the season: play for the school team, take the coaching, don't argue. Aidan had agreed to it in September because his father wanted him out of the house and doing something, and because Lyna had said, offhandedly, that basketball was just probability you could watch.

Lyna didn't play. She sat in the third row of the bleachers with a notebook and kept a tally of every shot Aidan took in practice, makes and misses, and she had opinions. The night before this practice she had texted him a link and then a wall of messages, and he had read them twice in bed with the screen brightness turned low. In 2018, two economists, Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo, had shown that the famous 1985 hot-hand analysis had a statistical bias, and had found evidence of streak shooting in the same data. He read it slowly. The same data. Whatever had convinced everyone for thirty years that the hot hand was a myth had been wrong, and the proof of that wrongness had been sitting in the old numbers the whole time.

At practice he was cold, though. Everything clanged. Mr. Menon, a square man with a whistle scarred from chewing, told him to stop thinking and let the game come to him, and when Aidan mentioned the study, the coach's expression ossified into something older and more certain than listening. "There is no hot hand," Mr. Menon said. "You make three in a row, you think you're special. You're just a coin."

"I'm not a coin," Aidan said. "Coins don't have tired legs."

The coach made him run suicides for that, which was fair, and Aidan ran them, and on the fifth sprint his thighs burned and his thoughts went thin and friable, breaking apart whenever he tried to hold more than one of them. Viviane, who played point guard and had overheard the whole exchange, caught him at the water fountain afterward. "You told Menon that shooting streaks are real," she said. "That's like telling a priest there's no such thing as prayer."

"It's not faith," Aidan said. "It's a paper. They looked at the old data and found the bias."

"Then prove it," she said. "You can't prove it by going two for twelve."

He knew that. The problem was that he also knew the opposite thing, the thing his body knew, which was that some nights the rim looked enormous and generous and other nights it looked like a mailbox slot, and that the difference did not feel random. Two truths were sitting in him at once and refusing to shake hands. Lyna's data said streaks were real, statistically, in the aggregate, over hundreds of shots by players he would never meet. His own five cold misses said nothing at all, one way or the other, and he had been treating them all season as though they were a verdict.

That was the part he couldn't stop turning over. He had spent the fall believing his slumps meant something about him, some defect that practice would eventually grind away, and the attrition had been real, hours dissolving into rebound drills, his outside shot sacrificed to the coach's system. Maybe Menon was wrong about the statistics and right about the boy in front of him. Maybe both. Miller and Sanjurjo had shown that a whole field could misread its own evidence for decades, and if that could happen to economists, it could happen to a seventeen-year-old counting his own failures in the dark.

The next game was a Tuesday, away, the bleachers half empty. In the third quarter Aidan hit a midrange jumper off a screen, then another on the catch, and then, when Viviane found him in the corner with the shot clock bleeding down, a third, and the feeling arrived the way weather arrives, unearned and unmistakable. Mr. Menon, who had not looked at him for two quarters, was suddenly shouting his name and drawing plays through him. Aidan took the fourth shot because he was supposed to, because the streak said so, and it went in off the back rim, soft, lucky, and he ran back on defense without celebrating, because he genuinely did not know what he had just proven.

Between the third and fourth quarters, Lyna came down from the stands and stood at the edge of the huddle, notebook against her chest. "Twelve attempts, four makes, all four consecutive," she said to him, quietly, while the coach drew arrows on his clipboard. "It's not evidence. But it's not nothing, either." Mr. Menon clapped once for attention and pointed at Aidan, and told the team the ball would go through the hot hand.

story:
Evan scraped a bin of grey rice into the compost bucket behind Marigold Kitchen and tried not to look at how full it was getting. He had taken the summer dish job to save money for a car that was beginning to feel theoretical, but the real education was happening in the walk-in, where Ms. Islam, the owner, kept her prep lists taped to the door. On Sunday nights she planned every dish the restaurant would serve that week, ordered exactly what each dish required, and cooked the bases in batches on Monday: stocks, braised beans, three sauces. Nothing sat unused for long. Evan had never seen anything so deliberate in his life.

"You're staring at my lists again," Ms. Islam said on his break, sliding him a bowl of the chickpea stew that had been Sunday's plan and Tuesday's lunch. "You want to write yours?"

"My mom works nights now," Evan said. "Nobody shops. We just, like, buy things."

"Then start with what you already throw away," she said. That evening he opened the fridge at home and counted: a slime-bagged cucumber, half a loaf gone blue at the edges, a tub of yogurt two weeks past its date, and a bag of carrots so soft they had bent inside the drawer. He stood there a long time with the door hanging open.

He told Zion about it at school, half embarrassed, because Zion had opinions about everything and delivered them like verdicts. "You're going to become one of those guys who proselytize about leftovers," Zion said, but he said it while pulling up something on his phone. "Look. My sister did a paper on this. A UN Environment Programme report found that 1.05 billion tonnes of food were wasted in 2022." He turned the screen toward Evan. "And about 60 percent of that waste happened in households. Households. Not restaurants, not farms. Us."

"Not us," Evan said. "Me. That fridge is a crime scene."

Melanie, who had been listening from the next desk, leaned over. She wanted in, though her reason was her own: she'd been trying to convince her father that she could handle a real kitchen before she left for her culinary program in the fall, and a week of planned, batch-cooked dinners would be her exhibit A. "Saturday we shop," she said. "Sunday we cook. Your kitchen or mine." Evan agreed before he could think of a reason not to.

On Saturday they walked the grocery store with a single list and a rule: nothing enters the cart without a meal attached to it. Evan found it was like learning a syntax, an order beneath the chaos; protein here, vegetable there, each item a word that only made sense inside its sentence, the week's dinners. Melanie argued for tofu, he argued for chicken thighs because Ms. Islam had taught him they forgave mistakes, and they compromised on both. His total at the register was less than what his family usually spent on two panicked, unstructured trips.

Sunday they cooked in his kitchen, and it was harder than the restaurant because there was no Ms. Islam and no second pair of industrial hands. A pot of rice scorched while they argued over whether the chili needed more cumin. But by evening the counter held five labelled containers, the fridge looked organized in a way it never had, and when his mother came home at midnight she stood in front of it for a full minute before saying, "Who are you and what have you done with my son."

The honest part, the part Evan did not say out loud to Zion's sister or anyone, was that he still didn't know if one family's neat containers mattered against a number with nine zeroes in it. Maybe the difference was real and maybe it was symbolic, a way of feeling clean while the world went on wasting, and he could not prove which. What he knew was smaller and concrete: on Thursday, when his mother texted him a photo of an empty container with the words where did the chickpea thing go, he stood in the restaurant's kitchen grinning at his phone, and Ms. Islam glanced over from the stove and said, "That's the face of a cook. Now come taste this stock and tell me if it needs salt."

story:
Amelia taped the drill sheets to the fence at nine in the morning, before the heat could sequester itself under the porch and before any of the ten-year-olds arrived and asked her questions she could not answer yet. The backyard was her mother's idea, offered the way her mother offered things, casually, as if the permission were the smaller part of the favor. The club had no field for a junior coach who was herself still on a high school roster, so the backyard it was: two Pop folding goals, a strip of grass worn thin in the middle, and eight small players who could not complete a pass across a ten-foot gap under any pressure at all. That weakness was her assignment. Mr. Hoffmann, who ran the club's junior program, had handed her a roster and one sentence. Fix the passing, he said. The rest is yours.

She had coached them the way she had been coached, which was to say loudly and constantly. A pass went astray and she was already calling out the flaw before the ball stopped rolling. Plant foot, she called. Open your hips. Look first, then play. Jadyn, who had come over to watch and eat a peach on the porch steps, counted silently for a while and then held up both hands, ten fingers spread. Amelia ignored her. The kids were listening, after all, nodding at every correction, and by the end of the first session the passing in the drills had actually looked cleaner. She wrote good session in her notebook and underlined it twice.

The trouble surfaced on Saturday, in the game. Amelia stood on the sideline with her notes and watched her players come apart the moment the whistle blew. Balls skipped off shins, passes went straight to the other team, and the small girl with the red cleats turned to the sideline after every single mistake, face blank, waiting for a voice that was not allowed to come. Nobody corrected them from the fence. The rules of game day held her behind a painted line, and without the corrections they seemed unable to find anything themselves. They lost five to one, and on the walk home Amelia turned her notebook over in her hands without opening it.

She did not want to tell Jadyn what she suspected, so she said it to the grass instead, on Sunday, restacking the cones she had left out overnight. I think it was me. Jadyn sat down on the porch rail, unhurried, and asked the question Amelia had been avoiding. How. Amelia laid two cones ten feet apart and looked at the space between them as though it held an answer. Every time they touched the ball I told them what went wrong. They never had to know for themselves. She said it and immediately hated the size of it, the way it reorganized the whole two weeks behind it.

That night she searched on her laptop until she found it, a phrase used by researchers who studied how people learn movement. It was called the guidance hypothesis. She read it three times, then closed the screen, then opened it again. The idea was simple and awful: feedback after every single attempt could make learners dependent on it, so less frequent feedback often helped retention. She copied nothing down. She wanted to carry it in her head the way you carry a suspicion.

Monday she changed everything and told no one, not even Jadyn, which produced a low current of secretiveness in the week, an incipient gulf between them that Amelia noticed and let stand. She broke the players into pairs and gave each pair a card. Two touches, one pass, check your own plant foot, she said, and then, deliberately, she walked to the far fence and stood there. For the first ten minutes it was worse than the game had been. Passes caromed off the gate, off the compost bin, off the dog that belonged to the neighbor and had learned to lie in the shade of the goal. Red cleats turned to the sideline twice, found nothing, and turned back.

Then Marianne, the smallest and most quietly stubborn of the eight, stopped a rolling ball with the sole of her foot and said to her partner, without raising her voice, "You're stepping on your plant foot every time." Amelia heard it from thirty feet away and felt something shift in her chest. The partner adjusted. The next pass was flat and true, and neither of them looked up. They had started doing her job for her, and it was better than her job, because it arrived inside the game instead of outside it.

On Thursday Mr. Hoffmann came to watch, unannounced, standing at the back gate with his arms crossed for twenty minutes while Amelia said almost nothing. Afterward he asked her what she was doing differently, and she considered lying, or hedging, and instead told him plainly: she had been correcting every pass, and now she held most of it back. He nodded once and left without saying whether it was right, and she understood that the next game would decide it, or would not.

Saturday came, hot and still. In the seventh minute, red cleats received a ball in traffic, and the whole sideline went silent, coaches and parents both, because everyone on her team had learned that no voice was coming. The girl took a touch, lifted her head, and struck a pass across the gap, ten flat feet of grass, straight to Marianne's run. Amelia's hands closed around the fence wire and did not let go.

story:
Jeremy had read the study twice, once on his phone in the parking lot and once at the counter while the cashier scooped his change out of the drawer. In 1999, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh had found that people liked a partner more when that partner quietly mimicked their posture and gestures, even without noticing the mimicry. He'd transcribed the sentence into his notes app under a heading he immediately regretted, which was PLAN, and now Carley was walking across the lot toward the shop with her thumbs hooked in her jacket pockets.

They ordered at the window. She got a waffle cone of pistachio, which struck him as an obdurate choice for a first date, the flavor nobody's relatives liked, and he copied her before he could decide whether he was copying her. When she leaned her elbows on the counter, he leaned his elbows on the counter. When she tilted her head to read the topping list upside down, he tilted his. It was working, or something was working, because she laughed at his joke about the plastic cow on the roof and said, "You're easier to talk to than most people," and his chest went warm and strange.

The trouble started at the picnic table. She sat with one ankle crossed under the bench, so he crossed his ankle under the bench, and she caught it. Not accusingly. She just looked at his feet, then hers, then his again, and said, "We're sitting the same way," and he felt the whole afternoon tilt like the topping list.

He had two thoughts at once, and neither would politely wait for the other. The first was that Keira had been right when she'd said, over biology homework, "People liked a partner more when the partner mimicked their posture and gestures, and they didn't even notice it, Chartrand and Bargh, 1999, it's in the textbook," before going back to her Punnett squares. The second thought was that a person who did it on purpose was doing something the study had never tested. The researchers hadn't measured whether the liking survived if you found out. Jeremy was not a phenotype, whatever Ms. Szabó said about his stubborn chin showing up in three generations of yearbook photos; he was a person making a choice at a picnic table, and the choice had a smell to it, faint but unmistakable, like the fake vanilla they pumped onto the sundaes.

Carley had switched to scraping the pistachio down toward the cone, short deliberate strokes, and he realized he was holding his spoon the same way, matching her rhythm, and that he had been for a while without deciding to. That undid something. Half of it was strategy and half was just his body drifting toward hers like water finding a level, and he couldn't cleanly separate the halves, and maybe nobody could.

"I have to tell you something dumb," he said.

She kept scraping. "Okay."

"I read a study. If you copy how someone sits, they like you more, and they don't notice. Keira told me about it and I looked it up and I've kind of been doing it. On purpose. Some of it." He heard how it sounded and kept going anyway. "Not all of it. Some of it my arms did without asking me."

She finished her cone down to the last square of waffle and looked at him for a long enough moment that he could hear the freezer case humming behind the window. Then she uncrossed her ankle and put both feet flat on the ground, deliberately, like someone rearranging pieces.

"That's so weird," she said. "Because I noticed you leaning on the counter like me and I thought, okay, he's nervous, that's fine, and then I started doing it back." She folded her arms, unfolded them, and put her hands flat on the table where he could see them. "So now neither of us knows which way we actually sit."

"That's the part that's making me insane," Jeremy said, and to his surprise she laughed, hard, the kind that involved the shoulders.

"Sit however you want," she said. "I'll like you or I won't, and you'll find out, and it won't be because of the study." She pushed her empty cone wrapper into a triangle and stood up. "Walk me to my car before my ice cream wears off. I want to show you the absolutely cursed playlist I made for the drive here."

He stood, and his body chose its own posture, whatever that was, and followed her across the lot.

story:
The bus dropped them at the gate of the decommissioned missile site just after ten, and Ms. Buchanan counted heads twice before letting anyone off the gravel path. Kayla carried her notebook against her chest, because the notebook was the reason she had signed up for the trip and she was not going to leave it on a bus. Inside, the silo had been converted into a walking exhibit, glass cases along the corridor, a decommissioned launcher bolted to the floor under lights, the whole place cold in a way that felt deliberate, as though the curators wanted visitors to understand that this was what the machinery required.

Her essay was due Monday. She had Gaddis down, or thought she did: the Cold War as a contest that settled into place because neither side could afford to lose, the long peace held by fear. Ms. Buchanan had written "One historian is not a debate" at the bottom of her draft in green ink, and Kayla had spent four evenings in the public library trying to find a second voice, coming home each night with her ambition slightly desiccated, thinner than when she'd left.

Sidney caught up with her at the case holding the launch keys, two of them, small and yellowed under glass. "You're doing the face again," Sidney said. "The essay face."

"I need a counterweight to Gaddis and I keep finding people who agree with him under different names."

"Try the shop," Sidney said. "They had actual books, not just keychains."

The shop was a counter at the end of the corridor with a rack of paperbacks, mostly memoirs and picture volumes. Morgan was already there, flipping through a book about submarines. Kayla worked down the shelf with her finger. Between a biography of a pilot and something about the Berlin Wall she found a thick blue spine, A Preponderance of Power, and pulled it out, and read the back cover standing in the aisle.

"Morgan," she said. "This is it. Leffler. He won the Bancroft Prize for this in 1993." Morgan looked at her with polite blankness. "It's the big one," Kayla said. "For history. Ms. Buchanan mentioned it once like it was the Oscars."

She read the summary standing up, one hand on the shelf. Leffler argued that American leaders had pursued national security through dominance of the postwar world, and the sentence stopped her, because it sounded at first like agreement with Gaddis, both of them describing a country that wanted to be safe, until she read it again. Fear of the Soviets was one explanation. The pursuit of dominance was another thing entirely, a choice about means and not only a response to threat. She turned the book over, then back, reading the same paragraph a third time as though the words might rearrange themselves.

She paid eleven dollars for the used copy, and outside, at the overlook above the empty launch apron, she found Sidney on a bench and sat down with the book open on her knees. The apron below was cracked concrete with weeds in the seams, and she thought of Gaddis writing about a world divided along tectonic lines, halves grinding against each other, and then of Leffler, writing about one of the halves deciding it would rather sit on the fault.

"So what's the difference, actually?" Sidney asked, leaning over. "Both of them think America wanted to be secure."

"Watch," Kayla said, and it worked exactly as it should have. "Gaddis says the rivalry locked in because each side saw the other as a threat. Leffler says the Americans chose dominance, that being preponderant was the strategy itself. If he's right, then even if the threat had been smaller, they'd still have wanted the upper hand." She tapped the page. "That's not a mood. That's a policy."

"Which one do you believe?"

Kayla didn't answer right away. She looked down at the apron, at the spot where the ground crews had once worked and where a magpie was now walking as if it owned the place. "The evidence problem," she said finally. "It's not just what happened. It's what counts as knowing why it happened. Leffler can show what the planners wrote down. Gaddis can show what the constraints were. Neither of them was in the room."

"That sounds like a no."

"It sounds like a maybe, weighted toward Leffler for the documents and away from him for the inference. Ms. Buchanan says an essay can hold a position and still say where the floor gives out."

Sidney squinted at her. "Floor gives out? That's grim, even for you."

"Epistemology," Kayla said. "Sort of. How you know the thing you claim to know. I looked it up Tuesday for fun and then it ruined my week." She wrote a line in her notebook, crossed it out, wrote it again, and underlined one word, and the magpie lifted off the concrete and cleared the fence in three wingbeats.

Ms. Buchanan called them back toward the bus at one o'clock, and Kayla walked with the book pressed flat under her arm, already composing the second paragraph in her head, the one that would begin: Against Gaddis stands Leffler, whose prize-winning account refuses the comfort of a shared deadlock. Behind her, Morgan called, "You're doing the face again," and Kayla, without turning around, said, "Good face. Keep it."

story:
The argument started before the bell finished ringing, the way arguments in fourth period always did, with Ricky leaning back in his chair like he had already won. "It doesn't matter," he said. "Young people don't vote. Half of them, tops. My brother says elections get decided by old people in Ohio."

"That's not what half means," Joanie said. She had her laptop open already, which meant she had been waiting for this. "CIRCLE estimated it. It's this research center at Tufts University. Fifty percent of Americans aged eighteen to twenty-nine voted in the 2020 presidential election. Fifty percent. That's millions of people."

"Millions of people who got outvoted by other millions of people," Ricky said, and a couple of kids near the window laughed.

Jacob said nothing. He was eighteen as of October, the oldest in the grade because his parents had held him back a year in kindergarten, and in two weeks there was an election, and he had not registered. He had meant to. He had picked up the form at the library in September and carried it in the front pocket of his backpack for a month, where it had gone soft at the corners like a leaf. The online deadline was today at midnight. He had checked that much. What he had not checked was whether the form in his backpack was still worth anything, or whether the paper deadline had already passed days ago and he had missed it by carrying it around like a talisman instead of mailing it.

Ms. Kelly let the argument run, walking the aisles the way she did, hands clasped behind her. "Jacob," she said, stopping at his desk. "You've been quiet. You're eighteen. What do you think?"

"Is fifty percent good or bad?" he said. It wasn't an answer, and he knew it, but it was the honest question. Half showed up and half didn't, and depending on which half you were in, the number looked like a miracle or an indictment.

"That's the wrong question," Ricky said. "The right question is whether it matters."

"Everything matters at the margin," Joanie said. "That's the whole point of a margin."

Jacob turned the form over in his mind, the paper one, soft-cornered, possibly dead. He could sublimate the worry into the argument, take a side, be loud about it, and half the class would think he was confident. Or he could admit the thing he had not admitted to anyone, which was that his father, who had opinions about every election and had never missed one, had told him last spring that voting was a habit you either started or didn't, and Jacob had nodded and put the form in his backpack, and that was the whole of his civic life so far.

After class Joanie caught him at the door. "You didn't say anything," she said. "For like ten minutes. That's weird for you."

"The paper deadline might be gone," he said. He said it quietly, so Ricky wouldn't hear, so nobody would hear. "I don't know if I missed it."

Joanie looked at him for a second with an unnerving perspicacity, like she could see the form through the canvas of the backpack. "There's a table outside the gym," she said. "The League of Women Voters or somebody. They've been there since Tuesday. They have laptops."

The hallway outside the gym was loud with the end of the day, and the table was small, one folding table, two women with a banner that kept sliding down the wall. Jacob stood in line behind a freshman who was only preregistering, too young for this election but doing it anyway, which struck Jacob as either very hopeful or very embarrassing depending on how you looked at it, and he still hadn't decided which when it was his turn.

"Eighteen?" the woman at the laptop asked.

"October," he said. He gave his name, his address, his license. His hand was unsteady on the trackpad in a way that embarrassed him, this embryonic civic identity of his trembling at the moment of its actual birth. The form in his backpack, he realized, could stay there forever now, a relic of the person who almost didn't.

"Hit submit," the woman said, and turned the laptop toward him.

The confirmation came up green. Behind him the line shifted, and out in the hallway Ricky was telling somebody, loudly, that it was all decided by old people in Ohio anyway. Jacob slid the laptop back, zipped his backpack over the dead form, and walked straight toward the sound of Ricky's voice.

story:
The testing center smelled like the inside of a new laptop, which Kate found appropriate, since the SAT had decided to become one. On the morning of her second attempt, the proctor sequestered their phones in a gray cabinet, lined them up like evidence, and Kate took her seat with the borrowed stylus balanced across her knuckles, waiting for the screen to decide something about her future.

The first math module went fine. Better than fine. She finished with six minutes left and spent them checking, which was its own kind of arrogance. Then the second module loaded, and the questions were absurd, unfamiliar shapes folded into unfamiliar questions, and somewhere around question nine she stopped being a person solving problems and became a person watching herself fail. She guessed on the last four. In the parking lot afterward she sat on a parking block and texted Axel: "second module was brutal. it's over. i'm going to community college and living in your garage."

Axel called her back instead of texting, which was how she knew he thought she was being dramatic. "Wait," he said. "How was the first module?"

"Easy. Why does that matter, the second one counts too."

"Kate. It's adaptive. The digital SAT is adaptive. It switched over in March of last year, in the US. How you do on the first module of each section sets the difficulty of the second one."

She sat with that on the parking block while a bird regarded her from the fence. "So if the second module was harder..."

"Then maybe you did well on the first. They don't give the hard questions to people who bombed the easy ones."

"That's a deranged way to run a test."

"It's an efficient way to run a test. Same thing."

She wanted to believe him, and noticed that wanting had very little to do with it. The logic held, she thought, the way a bridge holds when you drive over it slowly, but there was no way to stand underneath and check the bolts. She might have done well on the first module and earned the hard second one. Or she might have done well on the first module and then fallen apart completely on the hard second one, which was, when she examined it, exactly what had happened. Both things could be true. She hated that both things could be true.

Scores came out on a Tuesday, during sixth period, which meant she spent Mr. Van Dijk's class on the physics of momentum while her phone sat in her bag like a small bomb. Mr. Van Dijk drew a cart rolling down a ramp and said, "Once it's moving, the question is only what stops it," and Kate thought, thank you, that's very helpful, and did not raise her hand to point out that some forces were invisible and also unphotographable.

She checked in the hallway after the bell, walking fast so Malik, who was trailing her and narrating his own college essay out loud, wouldn't see her face. The number was good. Not transcendent, not the number she'd once taped inside her locker during a fit of ambition in sophomore year, but good, better than March, good enough that the hard second module had evidently not been the catastrophe she'd replayed for eleven days. She stopped walking. Malik ran into her.

"Why'd you stop? I'm mid-sentence. My essay is about my phenomenology of moving houses, which is a real word, my brother says it's the study of experience, so don't."

"Nothing," Kate said. "Good nothing."

"You got your score."

"I got my score."

Malik looked at her for a long second, which was more attention than he usually paid to anything that wasn't about Malik. "So is this a celebrating face or a face where you need me to buy you a pretzel."

"Undecided," she said, which was true, and also the first honest thing she'd said about college in a month. Her application was due in nine days. The essay was still an inchoate pile of paragraphs about her grandmother's garden that she had been afraid to shape into anything, in case shaping it revealed that there was nothing underneath. She had been treating the whole process like a verdict, she realized, standing there in the hallway: some external judgment that would arrive and tell her who she had already been all along. Axel's phone call had suggested a different model, a more unsettling one, where the test itself changed shape depending on what you showed it first, where difficulty might be evidence of something rather than proof against you. She didn't know yet whether she believed the second model. She only knew that when she'd thought the hard module meant failure, she'd been wrong, and that being wrong in that particular direction had cost her eleven days of thinking she was finished.

That night she opened the garden essay, deleted the first paragraph, and wrote a new one about a thing that had actually happened, which was that she had quit piano at eleven and regretted it in a way she'd never said out loud to anyone. It was riskier. It could be bad. She kept typing anyway, and outside her window the neighbor's sprinkler came on with its little mechanical gasp, and the cursor moved right.
