story:
The community theatre smelled of dust and hot glue, and Lucas sat in the third row with his notebook open to a page he had crossed out four times. Ms. Chatterjee had given them until Friday: a ten-minute play drawn from a moment in their own lives, staged on the little plywood platform that passed for a stage at the summer workshop. Nine days. Lucas had spent three of them not writing.

The problem was not invention. The problem was ownership. He had the scene in his head already, the one from last winter when his father had driven two hours through snow to watch Lucas fail an audition, and the silence in the car afterward had been more eloquent than anything Lucas could compose. It was the best material he had. It was also, in some way that he could not articulate, material he did not want anyone else to touch. Sahana had already read half the room's drafts aloud in her loud, delighted voice, offering notes on everything. Kayleb had asked, twice, whether he could "borrow the structure" of whatever Lucas was doing. Lucas had been reticent both times, which Kayleb seemed to read as permission.

"You're hiding it," Sahana said, dropping into the seat beside him on Wednesday. She pointed her chin at the notebook. "Nobody hides a script unless they think it's good, or unless they're stalling. Which is it?"

"Neither. I just don't want it stolen." He said it and immediately heard how paranoid it sounded. She raised one eyebrow and waited, the way she did in debates, letting the silence do the arguing.

"Stolen how? Kayleb would literally steal your dead grandpa's eulogy and perform it worse. That's not theft, that's tribute." She laughed, then stopped when he didn't. "Wait. You actually think someone would take it. Like, claim it?"

That night Lucas looked it up, partly to prove her wrong and partly because the question had begun to itch. He found forum threads, a government FAQ page, the website of a playwright whose ten-minute pieces he had admired since sophomore year. The answer came back so plainly he read it twice: a play is protected by copyright automatically, in the United States and in many other countries, as soon as it is written down. No registration. No form, no fee, no official envelope sealed and mailed to himself, which was the trick his uncle swore by for song lyrics. The page sat open on his phone while he ate cold rice, and he kept wondering whether it could really be that easy, whether something so fragile as a script could be guarded the instant it touched paper.

"It's automatic," he told Kayleb the next morning, in the lobby where the vending machine hummed like a distant highway. "The whole thing. You write it down and it's protected. In the U.S. and a bunch of other countries, right away, no registration needed." Kayleb blinked at him, and Lucas realized he had answered a question Kayleb had never asked aloud, which was its own kind of confession.

"So I couldn't take it," Kayleb said slowly.

"You couldn't take it and call it yours. Legally." Lucas turned his coffee cup in his hands. "I looked it up."

"I wasn't going to." Kayleb's voice had gone careful, the way it did when he was deciding whether to be offended. "I asked about structure because I liked what you did with the car scene at the reading. I heard you do the hallway monologue last week." He paused. "Is that what you think of me?"

And there it was, the thing underneath the thing. Lucas had assumed his fear was practical, a filing problem, a matter of envelopes and forms, and the filing problem had dissolved in one search. What remained was something less tidy: he had wanted the excuse. Guarding the script had given him a reason not to finish it, not to hand his father's silence to strangers in folding chairs. He tried to prognosticate, half-jokingly, how the showcase would go, what the audience would do with the most private ten minutes of his year, but the predictions kept collapsing into the real question, which was whether he wanted witnesses at all.

"I didn't think that of you," he said finally, and it was mostly true. "I think I thought it of me."

Ms. Chatterjee called them into the house at ten for blocking, and Lucas sat with his notebook while the others arranged chairs into a car, two rows of metal facing forward, Sahana in the passenger seat pretending to steer. He watched her hands find the wheel, watched Kayleb lean over and mime cranking a heater that didn't exist, and he understood something he could not have drafted in outline form: the script was already protected, had been since the first crossed-out page, but protection and performance were opposites in the way that mattered. One kept a thing closed. The other required opening it.

He uncapped his pen. In the margin of the fifth draft he wrote "Friday, 8:00, two chairs," and underneath, the first new line in a week: "The snow's still coming down. We should stay another night." Sahana looked over his shoulder, said nothing, and dragged a second chair to center stage.

story:
The basement of Grandpa Amos's house smelled of cedar shavings and old newsprint, and it was there, on the third Saturday of the school year, that Zachary spread his materials across the card table: a photocopy of Leviticus 19, a yellow legal pad, and his laptop open to the debate topic, which asked whether the Sabbath commandment still bound people in a society that had largely stopped observing it. He had until Thursday to argue the affirmative, and he had no idea how.

"Cheyenne's coming at four," his grandfather said from the bottom of the stairs, holding two mugs of coffee. "She called while you were setting up. Says she wants to practice against you."

"That's backwards. She's on the negative. She doesn't need to beat me, she just needs to make me look wrong."

"Then you'd better not be wrong." Grandpa set down the mugs and lowered himself into the folding chair, his knee popping like a knuckle. "Read it to me, the verse. The actual words."

Zachary read aloud, the command to keep the Sabbath holy, to do no work, that it applied to the Sabbath, to sons and daughters, to servants, to the stranger within the gates. When he finished, his grandfather was quiet for a while, turning his mug in slow degrees, and Zachary recognized the silence as a habit of the man's, a way of making a young person uncomfortable enough to keep talking.

"It says the stranger within your gates," Zachary said. "That's the immigration angle. Cheyenne will say the whole thing is a synecdoche, one rule standing in for an entire ancient worldview nobody holds anymore, so keeping it literally is like keeping a moth collection because you once loved butterflies. It doesn't disenfranchise anyone to stop, but it might disenfranchise people to enforce it, because whose rest counts and whose doesn't? Retail workers, nurses. That's her opener. I've heard her use it."

"You've heard her," Grandpa said. "Have you heard yourself? What do you actually believe?"

"I believe I have to win Thursday."

"That's not a belief, that's a schedule."

When Cheyenne arrived, she came down the stairs two at a time with her own binder, and Zachary noticed she had printed his practice case from the team forum, his own sentences annotated in red. She took the chair opposite him without asking, which was their arrangement, and their friendship, and he had learned not to read anything into it.

"Ready?" she said. "Your constructive, then I cross-examine."

He gave his speech, the strongest version he could build: the commandment's language included the stranger, the servant, the animal, which meant it was never merely private piety but a structure of rest extended to the powerless, and any modern equivalent, fair scheduling laws, guaranteed days off, would be its metamorphic descendant, the same principle changed in form. Cheyenne listened with her pen not moving, which was her tell that she was actually listening instead of loading.

"Leviticus 19:30," she said. "You quoted 19:3 and 19:10 and stitched them together. But the chapter is about the whole holiness code, and you picked the two verses that sound like labor law and skipped the ones about mixed fabrics." She leaned forward. "You found in the text exactly what you already believed before you opened it. You read yourself into it."

"That's not a thing."

"It has a name. Exegesis is drawing the meaning out of the words and the context. Eisegesis is reading your own ideas into it. My pastor uses the distinction all the time." She said it lightly, almost gently, which was worse. "You did eisegesis, Zachary. You wanted the verse to be about worker protections, so it was."

He wanted to argue, and opened his mouth to, and then closed it, because the yellow legal pad was sitting right there with his notes, and the notes were all conclusions written before the citations, each verse labeled with the use he had already decided on. He turned the pad face down, as if that helped.

They drilled for another hour, and somewhere in it Annabella texted the team chat asking whether anyone had a framework for the negative that didn't collapse into relativism, and Cheyenne typed back a single line, busy, and put the phone away. Zachary noticed she kept her own notes turned toward herself the whole time, and understood that she was not only preparing to beat him; she wanted, plainly, to be the best debater in their class this season, and beating the affirmative case on a topic this visible was her way of getting there. He had his want and she had hers, and on Thursday they would sit across from strangers and each try to take something the other needed.

That night he stayed at Grandpa's, in the room that had been his father's, with the ceiling stain shaped like a hand. He worked with the pad flipped back over, but now he wrote the verses first and his claims second, in a different ink. Some of them still matched. The verse about the stranger in the gates still said what it said, and he could still build from it, but he had to build through the mixed fabrics and the rest of it, through the parts he didn't like, and when he tried, the case got smaller and harder and, he suspected, truer. He could not tell yet whether it would win. He wrote at the bottom of the page, in small letters so he could deny it later: not sure. Check context first.

At breakfast, his grandfather asked how it had gone, and Zachary said, "Cheyenne caught me reading into the text instead of out of it," and reached for the toast.

story:
Jade found the book while looking for the good folding chairs, wedged behind the water heater in her grandmother's basement beside a box of Christmas napkins. It was a school textbook, cloth-bound, its spine gone soft, with her grandmother's maiden name penciled inside the cover in a careful teenage hand. She carried it upstairs into the noise of the party, past cousins arguing about parking, and set it on the kitchen counter next to the potato salad.

Later, when the eating had slowed and the aunts had moved to the porch, Jade sat at the counter and opened the book to the chapter on the war. She had a test on that same war on Tuesday, which was the whole reason she had brought her own textbook to her grandmother's house in the first place, folded into her bag like contraband. She laid the two books side by side. Same war. Same dates. Everything else was different.

Her grandmother's book gave the war almost a page: the treaty, the borders redrawn, the flags. Her own book gave it nine pages, most of them about what happened to the people inside the borders, the ones who were moved and the ones who stayed and resented it. Jade read a paragraph from the old book and then the matching stretch in the new one, back and forth, the way you might compare two photographs of the same face taken years apart. How could two textbooks, both of them presumably written by people who knew what they were doing, produce two different wars?

"Whose is that?" her grandmother asked, coming in for more ice. She picked up the old book, turned it over, laughed once through her nose. "Lord. Mr. Novák would faint." Jade looked up, startled; Mr. Novák was her history teacher. Her grandmother explained that he lived three doors down when Jade's mother was small, before he moved across town, and that he used to argue with her about this exact book on this exact porch, thirty years ago.

"He kept saying it was propaganda for the winners," her grandmother said, spooning ice into her glass. "I kept saying it was the book I was graded on."

Jade texted Teresa a photo of the two covers side by side. Teresa texted back a single word, no context: "oof." Then a second message: "ask him which one is true." Jade typed "which one IS true" and then sat with the question, her thumb hovering, because she was starting to suspect it was the wrong question, or at least a question with a hinge in it.

She went out to the porch, where the trees along the fence undulated in the evening wind, and found her mother and an uncle talking about the year the family business almost failed. Her mother told it one way, her uncle another, and where the two stories diverged they argued amiably for ten minutes, citing different aunts, different receipts, a letter nobody could produce. Neither of them called the other a liar. They just had different sources and, Jade noticed, different things they wanted the story to justify.

She thought of a geology video Jaiveer had shown her in the library, a cliff face cut through by roads, each stratum a different color holding a different era. The war was like that, she guessed. The event itself was the rock; the books were the layers that had accumulated over it, each one laid down by whoever was alive and writing at the time, each one answering whatever questions that generation was asking. Her grandmother's book had been written close enough to the war that the borders still felt like the main event. Her own book was written by people far enough away, and with enough archives opened, to care about what the borders did to families. Maybe hers. Maybe her own book would look like a stratum to someone in fifty years.

On Monday she stayed after class and put both books on Mr. Novák's desk, side by side, open to the war. He put on his glasses. He was quiet long enough that she began to regret it, and then he said, "You've found your first historiography problem." She asked what that word meant, and he said, "The study of how history has been written, and how the interpretations have changed over time," and slid the old book toward himself like a plate of something he hadn't tasted in years.

"So which one do I write about on the test?" Jade asked.

"Whichever one you can argue," he said. "And tell me honestly what you still can't decide."

That night at dinner her mother asked how studying had gone, and Jade said she had spent an hour on the old textbook, which was not hers, written for her grandmother, who was not taking the test. Her mother gave her the look she gave when Jade's attention had gone somewhere unprofitable. Jade ate her noodles and thought about the disaffected uncle on the porch, the version of the business story he would still be telling at Thanksgiving, and about how a person could hold two wars in her head at once without either one collapsing.

She texted her grandmother the question she had been saving: "Did you believe the book when you were my age?" The reply took a while, the way her grandmother's replies did, and when it came it said, "I believed all my books. That's what being sixteen was." Jade smiled at the screen, set the two textbooks on her desk with the old one on top, and turned off the lamp.

story:
The foreclosure sign had been staked into Ms. Pritchard's lawn sometime between Tuesday and Thursday, and Camille had biked past it twice before she let herself stop. White placard, red letters, a phone number for some office in the county seat. She stood with one foot on the pedal and read it three times, as if the word might rearrange itself into something else. Ms. Pritchard had lived in that house since before Camille was born. She grew tomatoes along the side fence and once called herself, laughing, the street's resident raconteur, the one who remembered which dog had lived where and who had painted which door.

That evening Camille sat at the computer at home, her mother making dinner noises in the kitchen, and typed the word into the search bar. Foreclosure. The results came back fast, in the flat confident voice of the whole internet, and she read with her chin on her fist.

She learned that it worked like this: a mortgaged home is collateral for the loan. If the borrower stops paying, the lender can foreclose, which means taking the house and selling it to recover the debt. She read the sentence twice, then said it under her thumb where her mother couldn't hear, testing its weight. The house itself was the guarantee. You didn't just owe money; you had staked the place where you slept on the promise to pay it back. She thought it almost axiomatic once she saw it, so obvious that nobody had ever needed to say it out loud to her, and that was exactly what bothered her. What else was axiomatic that she hadn't been told?

"Camille, dinner in ten," her mother called.

She kept reading. Down payments, deposits, rent versus owning. When you rented, you paid a landlord every month and a deposit up front that came back if you left the place intact. When you bought, you saved a down payment, a fraction of the price, and borrowed the rest, and the rest was the mortgage, and the mortgage was anchored to the house itself. She opened a new tab and typed her own question into it, awkwardly honest: why do people lose houses.

The answer came back the same in different words, over and over. People lose jobs. People get sick. Payments stop. The lender forecloses. She thought about Ms. Pritchard's tomatoes, which had come in heavy this August, and the little wire cages she built herself out of fencing scraps. A house could be full of care and still be taken, because care wasn't currency. She tried to problematize that, to hold it up and turn it the way Mr. Whoever taught them in seminar: was it wrong, or just how lending worked, or both at once? She couldn't get the two ideas to sit still next to each other.

She texted Milena. Did you see the sign on Pritchard's lawn?

Milena called instead of texting back. "My dad says she missed payments after her sister died," Milena said, her voice low, like she was reporting something from a war. "The bank takes the house. It's called foreclosure. They sell it to get their money back."

"So it was never really hers," Camille said.

"It was hers. It was also the bank's, kind of, the whole time." Milena paused. "That's messed up."

"Or it's the only reason she could buy it at all," Camille said. "Nobody has the whole price in cash." She heard herself defending a mechanism she had learned forty minutes ago, and heard also that it didn't settle anything, that both things could be true and she was allowed not to know which one mattered more.

The next afternoon she biked over with a jar of her mother's soup, because soup was what her mother sent when there were no words. Ms. Pritchard answered the door in a cardigan despite the heat. On the phone behind her, someone from the bank was saying something about a date.

"Camille," Ms. Pritchard said. "Sit with me a minute. Tell me about your first semester. I want to hear everything about that college of yours."

Camille sat on the porch steps, the jar warm between her hands, and said, "I start in three weeks."

"Well," said Ms. Pritchard, and looked out at the sign.

story:
The Saturday market occupied half the closed-off street, and Anthony moved through it with his mother's list folded in his back pocket. At the poultry stall, Ross was wrapping a whole bird in paper for another customer, his hands quick and unbothered by the cold slick of the raw chicken. Anthony waited until the stall emptied.

"Six breasts," he said, and slid the money across. "I'm cooking tonight. Mom's covering someone's shift."

Ross picked out the package without ceremony. "First week here, the smell got to me. Touching it all day, the cold, the rinse water. Then you just get desensitized, like your hands forget to be disgusted." He weighed the breasts, then leaned in. "You cooking that? Make sure it hits 165 degrees Fahrenheit inside, about 74 Celsius. My boss makes me check every sample with a thermometer. That's what the food safety agencies say, 165 and it's safe."

"That's very specific."

"That's a health code and a paycheck." Ross grinned and added a sprig of rosemary to the bag without charging for it. "Get a thermometer, Anthony. Don't guess."

Two stalls down, Ms. Oliveira from the English department was buying bread, and she flagged him over the way teachers do, with a small wave that expected compliance. "Doing the family shopping? How domestic." She accepted her change and then nodded toward the crowd. "Everyone keeps telling me the market raised the parking fees on Saturdays. The market didn't raise anything. City hall did. But people say the market, and everyone knows what they mean. Metonymy, and sloppy thinking, all in one."

"Is that on the exam?"

"Everything is on the exam, Anthony, whether I write it there or not." She nodded at his bag. "Feed them well."

At home the kitchen was quiet except for the refrigerator's hum. His father had left a note on the counter: working late, back by eight, and beneath the note, sitting on top of the recipe book, an instant-read thermometer still in its plastic sleeve. Anthony had never seen it before. He searched the drawer for scissors, cut the sleeve, and turned the probe in his hand like a pen he wasn't sure how to hold. The sleeve carried a small printed card, and he read it twice, folding it into his pocket afterward.

He set the oven, salted the chicken, heated the oil until it shimmered, and laid the breasts in with a sound like applause. While they seared, he texted Alden, who replied with a photo of himself at the skate park and the message "cooked dinner once, never again." Anthony set the phone face down. When the first breast came out of the pan, golden on the outside, he did what he had always seen his mother do: he cut into the thickest part with the edge of the knife. The meat near the bone was faintly pink, and the juices ran cloudy, and he stood there with his knife in the meat and no way of knowing what the color meant. Pink could mean undercooked. Pink could mean nothing. He thought of Ross weighing packages with steady hands, certain about numbers instead of colors.

He wiped the probe, pushed its tip into the thickest breast at an angle toward the center, and watched the digital face climb. 140. 151. The numbers moved slowly, as if reluctant, while the chicken sat cooling on the board. 158. 164. The display settled at 166, then 167, and something in his chest unlocked. He tested the second breast, the third, the fourth, the way Ross checked every sample. All of them cleared 165 Fahrenheit, and he thought, irrelevantly, that if Ross were here he could say the Celsius conversion too, about 74, and sound like someone who knew things. The pink near the bone had not mattered; the number had.

He made rice and the green beans Ms. Oliveira had pointed him toward, set the table with the good plates because his father's note had also said it was the kind of week that deserved a real dinner, and put the thermometer through the washed chicken again at his elbow out of pure superstition. By seven forty-five the kitchen smelled like a kitchen in someone else's better memory of home. He had planned to be smug about it, and instead he felt only the large, plain hope that they would notice.

The door opened at eight, and his mother came in first, still in her work polo, holding a paper bag that leaked a spot of grease onto the hallway floor. She lifted it toward him like an apology already in progress. "The stall at the market was selling the roasted ones, and the line was short, and I didn't think you'd actually do it." Then she saw the table, the plates, the carved chicken arranged under foil with the rosemary laid across it, and she stood in the doorway holding a warm dinner in one hand while a warm dinner went cold behind him.

"Take it back to Ross tomorrow," his father said, taking off his coat. "Lunch."

"Ross will laugh so hard," Anthony said, and lifted the foil. "Eat this one first."

story:
The chemistry exhibit occupied the museum's third floor, between the butterfly conservatory and the planetarium, and Riley had walked past it a dozen times on school trips without stopping. Today he stopped, because tomorrow he stopped having a chance. Mr. Khan had made it plain in Friday's lesson: the retake on stoichiometry was Monday morning, first period, and Riley's first attempt had been a flat forty-two.

The exhibit was called "Counting the Invisible." A touchscreen let you drag a digital balance under a glass dome filled with dry ice, fog tumbling off it like something turgid and alive, and the screen would ask you how many moles of carbon dioxide you were looking at. Riley entered his answer, hit submit, and watched the screen flush red. Wrong. He tried again, wrong again, and felt the specific heat of embarrassment that comes from failing in public, even when the public is a machine.

"You're the guy who sits behind Jai," a voice said. Regan from his chemistry class stood at the next station, jacket sleeves pushed up, working the same screen with brisk certainty. "You failed the mole test too?"

"Forty-two," Riley said. "You?"

"Sixty-one. Close enough to hurt." She reached over and tapped his screen. "What did you put?"

He showed her his work. He'd written the molar mass of carbon dioxide as 12.01 plus 16.00, gotten 28.01 grams per mole, and divided from there.

"That's it," Regan said. "You forgot the CO2 has two oxygens. It's 12.01 plus two times 16.00. So 44.01 grams per mole."

Riley stared at the number on his scratch paper. He had copied the formula correctly, drawn the little subscript two, and then ignored it completely, as if the oxygen had brought a friend who didn't count. He erased, redid the arithmetic, divided the sample mass on the screen by 44.01, and submitted. The dome lit up green and a cheerful tone rang out, and something in his chest loosened that had been knotted since Friday.

They worked the stations together after that, trading mistakes. Regan forgot to convert grams before dividing; Riley dropped a decimal point and got an answer that claimed the dry ice dome held more moles than atoms in the room. A docent drifted by, an older man with a lanyard, and watched them argue over whether their numbers were even reasonable. "You two are doing more with this exhibit than most grad students," he said, and moved on without correcting anything, which Riley took as a good sign.

At the polymer display, the touchscreen explained that the plastic in a milk jug was built from repeating units called monomers, and Regan, who wanted to do materials engineering, spent ten minutes on that station while Riley waited, half annoyed and half grateful, because the mole practice had settled into his hands now, the way free throws do. He found he could do a problem in his head: mass, divided by molar mass, moles. He even caught himself starting to cogitate over a balancing problem two exhibits ahead, mapping it out before he'd reached the screen.

Here was the thing he couldn't decide, though, and he turned it over while Regan read about polyethylene. His father believed you learned math by grinding, at the kitchen table, worksheet after worksheet, no shortcuts. His older cousin believed you learned it by understanding, one clean idea at a time, no grinding at all. Riley had ground through two weeks of worksheets and failed anyway, and today one sentence from a classmate, two oxygens, 44.01 grams per mole, had moved something that all that grinding hadn't touched. So the cousin was right? Except the sentence wouldn't have landed if he hadn't ground, if he hadn't already known what a mole was and what the formula meant and where to put the numbers. Maybe it was both, braided together, the repetition building the floor the understanding stood on. He couldn't prove that. He only knew that tomorrow's retake would test it either way.

At closing time they rode down the escalator, and Regan checked her phone and said, "Wait, the retake is Monday? I thought it was Wednesday. I have the physics midterm Monday."

"It's Monday. Mr. Khan said first period."

She looked at the phone again, then at him, and something shifted in her face, the calculation of a person redoing her week on the spot. "Then we should come back here tomorrow. Bring real problems. You clearly can't be trusted alone with an oxygen."

Riley held the door for her into the cold parking lot, where the frost on the railings had begun to form its own faint white fog.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
story:
Brayden laid the driver's manual open on the kitchen table beside a cereal bowl he had washed but not dried, and turned to the page with the diagram of cones. Two sticks of butter stood in for the parked cars. He nudged a salt shaker between them and slid an orange across the counter, mimicking the curve of reverse, until his mother came in for her coffee and moved the orange to the fruit bowl.

"It's the test on Friday," he said. "Parallel parking and the merge onto the ring road."

"That's why the butter is in the middle of the counter." She said it without a question mark, and he liked her for that.

At school, Leanne had watched him mime the hand-over-hand turn of a steering wheel during free period and told him he should film the butter-and-orange method and monetize it, study guides for the driving test, five dollars a download. Philip, who had failed the same test twice, said the whole licensing system was a travesty designed to extract money from seventeen-year-olds, and that his sense of direction was congenital, inherited from a father who once drove to the wrong city. Brayden laughed, though privately he thought Philip was wrong about the test and right about the nerves. The test wasn't unfair. It was just precise, and precision could be learned.

His mother couldn't teach him; her licence had lapsed the year his father left. So on Thursday evening, Ms. Petrov from two doors down, who drove a small grey hatchback and had once taught swimming at the community centre, took him out. First the side street with the orange cones someone had left from a construction job. He backed between them four times, twice clipping the rear cone, once leaving the car angled like a boat at a dock. "That's a travesty," he said of the third attempt, and Ms. Petrov said, "Do it again," which was her way of agreeing.

The fifth time, the car slid in clean, tires close to the curb, and something loosened in his chest. He sat with his hands still on the wheel, memorizing the feeling of it, the way the cone had vanished from the side mirror at exactly the right moment.

Then the highway. The on-ramp rose ahead, long and curved, and he could see the traffic in the right lane coming toward him from behind, a delivery truck, then a gap, then a line of headlights. He waited, accelerated, and at the last second, as he was already drifting toward the lane, his hand found the signal stalk and flicked it on. The car in the gap braked, headlights flaring, horn short and sharp. Ms. Petrov's hand came off her knee but did not touch the wheel. He merged anyway, shaking, and drove.

"You signalled as you started the move," she said. "Too late. Signal before, so they know what you're going to do. That driver had no time to adjust." That was all she said, and it was enough. He thought of the butter sticks on the counter, how he'd slid the orange without announcing anything to anyone. On the next ramp he flicked the signal while the traffic was still a distant line of lights, watched the car in the lane ease back a car's length, felt the gap open like a door held for him. The third ramp he did without thinking first, and that was when he understood it wasn't about politeness, it was about time, giving other people the seconds they needed to decide. He had spent the week treating the test as a set of motions performed alone, cones and curb and mirrors, but the highway part could never be solo. The signal was a sentence spoken to strangers before the action, not after it.

Back in the kitchen that night, he closed the manual and set the butter back in the fridge. Leanne texted him a video she'd taken on the sidewalk, his fifth attempt, the clean one, and asked if she should post it. He watched the little grey car slide between the cones, thought of the headlights flaring on the ramp, the horn, the door opening on the third try. "Not yet," he typed. "Film the merge tomorrow after I pass." He put the phone face down on the counter and rinsed the orange under the tap, then stood eating it in sections by the window, looking out at the dark street where the cones still waited in a row.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
story:
Christopher had built the reading nook himself out of two armchairs angled toward the window and a lamp with a shade the color of weak tea, and he sat in it with The Catcher in the Rye open on his knee, having read the same page four times. The book smelled like the antiquity of every school library copy ever issued, which is to say like pencil shavings and other people's hands. On the windowsill, his phone lay face down, which was a form of protest he did not entirely believe in.

The essay question, assigned by Mr. Kim and due in two days, was one sentence long: "How does point of view shape the reader's trust?" Mr. Kim had a habit of assigning questions that fit in a fortune cookie and took a week to answer. Christopher had underlined it, boxed it, and then sat there doing neither, because he did not actually know what he thought.

The trouble was Holden. The trouble was that Holden had told him, on roughly the first page, "I'm the most terrific liar you ever saw in your life," and then gone on talking for two hundred more. Christopher flipped back to check that he hadn't invented the line. He hadn't. The Catcher in the Rye, published in 1951, opened with its narrator announcing himself a liar, which struck Christopher as roughly equivalent to a chef opening a restaurant by confessing to food poisoning.

He texted Sydney, who had already finished the essay. Sydney texted back a single thumbs-up, which prognosticated nothing except that Sydney was at dinner. Then he texted Ember, who replied three minutes later: "coming over. don't write anything yet."

Ember arrived with her own copy, a paperback so broken it opened by itself to the middle, and folded herself into the second armchair with her shoes on the cushion, which Christopher decided not to police. "Okay," she said. "How much of his story do you believe?"

"That's the question, isn't it. He tells us he lies. So do we believe the confession, or is the confession also a lie?"

Ember chewed the end of her pen. "Both. That's the whole thing. You can't throw out the book and you can't swallow it. He says he's the most terrific liar you ever saw in your life, and then he tells you about his dead brother, and that part feels true in a way he doesn't seem to notice."

Christopher wrote that down, then crossed out "seems to notice" because it was doing too much work. Outside, a leaf blower started up somewhere down the block and ran through what felt like an interminable autumn of its own. He said, "So the point of view isn't a window. It's a screen. We're not seeing his life. We're seeing what he does with it while he's telling it."

"Which is what Mr. Kim wants you to say but in your own handwriting."

"Mr. Kim wants everything in my own handwriting. It's his whole pedagogy."

Ember threw a pillow at him. He caught it badly and knocked the lamp, and the weak-tea light swung across the ceiling and settled. He picked the book back up and read a stretch aloud, the part where Holden describes someone as phony and then, two paragraphs later, does the exact thing he'd condemned, and Ember said "there, see," and Christopher said "wait, wait," and read it again.

Here was the position he worked out, slowly, with the pen cap in his teeth: Holden's lying wasn't a flaw in the story, it was the story, and the reader's trust wasn't something the narrator lost but something the reader had to keep renegotiating, page by page, the way you keep walking on ice that keeps creaking. What stayed uncertain, and he was honest enough with himself to leave it uncertain, was whether Holden knew he was doing it. Maybe the lies were armor and maybe they were just breath, and the text wouldn't tell him which, and he suspected the text was right not to.

He wrote until eleven, and Ember fell asleep in the second armchair with her sneakers still on and her own book open on her chest like a small roof. In the morning he would email Mr. Kim the draft and brace for the comment in red pen that fit in a fortune cookie. For now he set his pen down, reached over, and turned off the swinging lamp so she could sleep.

story:
Lily had not been nervous at the licensing office, which was the first thing worth noting, and it was only the trembling of her hands on the steering wheel now that made her reconsider whether she had been entirely honest about that. The parking lot behind the shuttered Kmart was vast and grey, its lines faded to a suggestion, like something diaphanous laid over the asphalt. Ms. Paquette, the instructor her mother had hired, sat in the passenger seat with a clipboard she never once wrote on, which Lily chose to interpret as confidence rather than indifference.

Two weeks earlier, waiting for her permit test, Lily had stood in that beige office and read a poster on the wall because Jana's texts had stopped coming and there was nothing else to look at. Drivers aged sixteen to nineteen, the poster said, had a fatal crash rate almost three times as high as drivers aged twenty and older, per mile driven. She had read it twice. A boy beside her, maybe fifteen, was quizzing his mother on road signs and getting them wrong with total serenity, and Lily had thought, not kindly, that the poster was really about him.

That night Jana had texted her a long message about why she hadn't gone through with signing up for the permit test herself, and Lily had read it under her covers with the screen brightness turned low, the way you read anything important. "I'm not saying I'm scared," Jana wrote, "I'm saying the numbers are the numbers, and you don't get to opt out of being a statistic by being special. My cousin rolled a car at seventeen and everyone still calls him the lucky one. Maybe I'll do it next year. Maybe the risk per mile goes down when you're twenty and I'll just wait it out. Anyway tell me how the Kmart lot is, you said that's where they teach you, that's so grim, I love it."

Lily had typed back a joke about the ghost of retail past and then deleted it, because it wasn't what she meant, and what she meant was harder to say: that she had taken the test anyway, and that she wasn't sure whether that made her brave or merely lucky in a way that hadn't resolved yet. She settled on "it's next week, I'll bring you a slushie after," which underwrote the whole arrangement between them, the promise standing in for the reassurance she couldn't manufacture.

"Gentle on the gas," Ms. Paquette said now, in the tone of someone describing weather. Lily's foot had been, in her own accounting, gentle. The car lurched and stalled, and the silence afterward had a texture to it. "Again. Turn the key. This time imagine you're pouring something you don't want to spill."

"That's a nice image," Lily said, restarting the engine. "My friend Jana thinks nobody our age should drive at all. She read the same poster I did."

"She's not entirely wrong," Ms. Paquette said, which Lily felt was a betrayal of the entire transaction. "Almost three times the fatal crash rate of anyone twenty or older, per mile. It's on the poster because it's on the data. Doesn't mean you stay home. Means you pay attention." She adjusted the mirror on her side, the way people do when they've decided the conversation is over.

They practiced turns between the faded lines, and Lily found she could do two things at once only if she stopped narrating them to herself, which was its own kind of quiet. On her fifth attempt at a three-point turn she thought of Saad, who had gotten his license at seventeen and driven everyone everywhere with an air of destiny, and how she'd once told him he drove like a lawsuit waiting to be filed. He'd laughed. She'd meant it, mostly. There was a small casuistry she'd been running for a year, telling herself that her caution was principle while his confidence was recklessness, when honestly she had just been afraid, and dressing fear up as judgment felt, in the empty lot, with the wheel warm under her hands, like the one thing she'd done that was genuinely dishonest.

The car crawled through the turn. She checked her mirror, checked it again, completed the maneuver without stalling, and Ms. Paquette said "adequate," which from her appeared to be a decoration for valor. Lily laughed, surprising herself, a short sound in the closed car.

"You can pull up by the cart corral and set the brake," Ms. Paquette said, checking her phone. "That's our hour."

Lily eased the car toward the corral, where a single shopping cart stood abandoned against the rail, listing slightly, and she brought the car to a stop a careful three feet from it, then, after a moment's thought, another foot closer. She pulled the handbrake and let her hands rest on the wheel, and outside the windshield the cart shifted in the wind, rolled a half-turn, and stopped.

"You'll book the next one?" Ms. Paquette asked, already gathering her clipboard.

"I'll text my friend first," Lily said, and reached for her phone on the passenger seat behind the instructor's bag.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
story:
The departures board turned over three times before the gate agent announced that the flight to Lisbon would be at least four hours late, and Payton sat down on the cold tile beside the window and opened her laptop on her knees. Mr. Tran had assigned the population profiles before winter break, one page per student, hers due by midnight no matter where in the world she happened to be. She had Portugal. She had meant to finish it on the plane.

Beside her, Moses was reading a guidebook with his feet stretched across their shared duffel bag, and Alexy had gone to buy sandwiches. The three of them were going to visit Alexy's grandmother for the holidays, an arrangement their parents had codified in a group email with rules about curfews and spending money, rules that Moses had already printed and annotated with jokes.

Payton's page needed one thing: a decision. Would Portugal in thirty years need more schools or more nursing homes? She had a printed copy of the country's profile chart folded into the front pocket of her backpack, and she spread it now on the tile, smoothing the creases with the heel of her hand. The chart looked like two towers standing back to back, bars of different lengths, numbers along the sides. She had assumed, from the first glance on the bus to the airport, that the left side showed females, because she was used to reading left to right and thinking of herself first. So she had started drafting a paragraph claiming the profile was bottom-heavy, wide at the base, young.

"The bars," Moses said, leaning over without invitation. "That's a population pyramid, right? My sister did one." He pointed at the stacked rows of ages. "Youngest at the bottom, oldest at the top, like a building."

"I know that part," Payton said. But she didn't know which side was which, and now she was worried she had it backwards, and the paragraph on her screen was built on a guess.

Alexy came back with sandwiches and dropped into the third chair. "Gate's a zoo," she said. "Some man tried to board with a fish tank." She looked at the chart. "What's the assignment?"

"Predict what the country needs. Schools or nursing homes." Payton turned the paper sideways, as if the problem would rearrange itself. The longer bars, the wide part, whichever sex that was, sat in the middle ranges, the forties and fifties, and the bottom of the chart was narrow. She knew what a narrow base meant if she let herself say it. Fewer young people. But if she had the sexes flipped, her whole reading of the imbalance flipped too.

Mr. Tran had told them, on the last day of term, that the assignment was less about Portugal than about how they reasoned. "Anybody can look up an answer," he had said. "I want to see the seeing." Payton had thought this was a teacher's way of making things harder than necessary. Now, with four hours of delay and a midnight deadline, she thought it might be the only useful thing he had said all semester.

She searched on her phone, holding it low so the screen glare wouldn't wash out, and found a page from a geography text with a caption underneath a similar chart. Males on the left, females on the right. She read it twice, then set the phone face down. So the left tower was males, the right females, and the ages stacked from youngest at the bottom to oldest at the top, exactly as Moses had said, and her draft paragraph had the sexes reversed. The asymmetry she had noticed, one side bulging more than the other in the middle years, belonged to the men, not the women. That mattered for the nursing homes question, she supposed, since women in most countries lived longer, and the chart showed that too, in the thin pale rows at the top where the female side stretched further.

She deleted the paragraph and started over. The wide middle, the narrow base, the long female tail at the top: put together, they pointed toward an older country, one that would be stocking pharmacies and building wards before it broke ground on primary schools. But she made herself write the counterweight as well, the honest part. A narrow base could recover; people moved; policies changed. A prediction was not a law of physics, more like a guess about a system trying to hold its own homeostasis, a population adjusting itself over decades in ways no single chart could codify. She wrote that she was confident about the direction and uncertain about the speed, and left it there.

"Done?" Moses asked, when she hit send at 9:40 p.m., one minute after the boarding call finally crackled through the terminal.

"Done enough." She folded the chart along its old creases and put it back in the front pocket. Alexy shouldered the duffel and Moses picked up the sandwich wrappers, and the three of them joined the slow, turbid line snaking toward the jet bridge, and Payton kept her boarding pass in her hand the whole way, uncreased.

story:
The gray came out of the tube the same way it always did, a plain slab of nothing, and Faith pushed it across the canvas in two long strokes before she noticed that the strokes did not match. On the left, where she had underpainted a field of raw orange, the gray sat warm, almost fleshy, like cement on a summer sidewalk. On the right, over a patch of scraped blue, the same paint went cold and steely, the color of a January morning. She held the brush above the canvas and did not move it. She had squeezed from one tube. She was sure of that, because she had squeezed it herself, ten minutes ago, in this room that smelled of turpentine and burnt coffee.

The community studio occupied the back half of a shuttered plumbing supply shop, and on Thursday evenings it belonged to whoever showed up with five dollars and a willingness to sweep at the end. Curtis had claimed the easel beside hers in September and never given it up, though he mostly painted girls he had no intention of speaking to. Tonight he was hunched over a portrait with the chin wrong again, and Hugh was at the window doing what Hugh always did, which was three careful marks and then twenty minutes of staring, as if the painting might confess something if he waited long enough.

"Come look at this," Faith said. "Tell me if I'm losing it."

Curtis leaned over, chewing the plastic end of a pen. "The gray's different. Did you mix two batches?"

"One tube. One squeeze. Watch." She dragged a fresh stroke across the boundary so that it crossed from the orange into the blue, and the stroke changed temperature in the middle like a road crossing a county line. Curtis made a low sound through his teeth. Hugh came over, looked for a long moment, and said, "It's the underpainting doing that. It has to be."

Faith wanted a better word than "has to be." She had wanted a better word all autumn, ever since her interview at the art school in the city, where a woman with gray-streaked hair had flipped through her portfolio and said it was promising but undisciplined, that she relied on accident and called it intuition. The sentence had catalyzed something in Faith that she still could not name, a stubbornness that made her want to prove the woman wrong and, in weaker moments, made her suspect the woman was right. The letter from the school was due any day now. She had stopped checking the mailbox because checking made her insufferable, her mother said, and her mother was not incorrect.

Mr. Banerjee, who ran the studio and had run it since before the plumbing shop closed, kept a shelf of warped art books by the sink. Faith went to it while Curtis and Hugh argued about whether the phenomenon had something to do with the lamp. Most of the books were water-damaged monographs, but one, fat and cloth-bound, had a spine she could read: Principles of color. She carried it to the folding table and let it fall open where it wanted.

There it was, in a chapter on a chemist named Michel Eugène Chevreul, who had published his law of simultaneous contrast in 1839. The page said that a color appears to shift toward the complement of the color placed next to it. She read the sentence twice, then a third time, mouthing it. Her gray had not changed at all. It had only done what a gray does beside orange and beside blue, pushed this way and that by its neighbors, faithful and deceptive at once.

"Simultaneous contrast," she said aloud, carrying the book back to the easel. "That's what it's called. A chemist figured it out. He published it in 1839."

"Wait, the color moves?" Curtis said.

"No. It looks like it moves. Toward the complement of whatever's beside it." She set the book down open on the stool. "So my gray isn't two grays. It's one gray getting pushed around."

Hugh peered at the page. "So you could plan it," he said slowly. "You could pick the underpainting to make the gray do whatever you wanted."

That was the turn of it, and Faith felt the turn happen in her chest. All term she had let the accidents stand, calling them happy, and part of her had known that the woman in the city was talking about exactly this. But the book said something more complicated than either accident or control. The gray was honest and the gray was a liar and both were true depending on the company it kept. She did not know yet what to paint with that knowledge, only that she had it now and could not give it back.

She worked until nine, laying a new ground of green under a strip of gray she had scraped clean, watching it flush faintly red as it dried. Curtis packed up his travesty of a chin and left without goodnight, which meant he was still angry about the portfolio review, where the visiting critic had praised Faith's accident and said nothing about his portrait. She let him go. It cost her something to let him go, and she paid it.

At the door, in her coat, she stopped and looked at the half-finished strip, green pushing the gray somewhere she had not predicted, her plan already drifting off its rails in a way she could not yet tell was failure. She took out her phone and photographed it, then photographed the open book beside it, Chevreul's name and the date and her one gray becoming many.

"Tomorrow," she said to the empty studio, "the mailbox."

story:
Peyton counted the thumbnails on her laptop screen for the third time, and the number stayed stubbornly at ten. She was sitting on the porch of the art cabin at Camp Windrow, mosquitos ticking against the porch light, her sketchbook balanced on her knees. Ten pieces. She had planned for ten all summer, a tidy arc around the theme of houses left behind, drawings of doorways and peeled wallpaper and the hollow where a porch swing used to hang. The plan had felt complete in June. Now, in the last week of July, it felt like a house with a missing wall.

She had heard about the AP portfolio from Kayden, who was already a senior and had a stack of college brochures on her bunk like playing cards. Kayden had mentioned it offhandedly over dish duty, scraping macaroni into the compost bin, and Peyton had filed it away and then, tonight, looked it up on the camp's one spotty computer. What she found made her sit very still.

"Sustained Investigation," Kayden said the next morning, when Peyton showed her the screen by the canoe rack. Kayden was wringing out a towel, and she squinted at the page. "That's the section they score. Fifteen digital images. Sixty percent of the whole thing." She tossed the towel over the rack. "You're doing ten."

"I was doing ten." Peyton looked down at the lake, where Talon was trying to teach a cluster of eleven-year-olds to paddle in something resembling a line. "Ten seemed like a real number. Enough to say something."

"Fifteen is the number that counts, apparently." Kayden picked at a splinter on the rack. "Anyway, you've got a year."

The morning passed in its ordinary rhythms, but Peyton kept doing the arithmetic in her head. Five more pieces. Five more doorways, five more empty rooms, and the ten she had already made would have to stretch further, mean more, sit beside five strangers she hadn't planned for. She found herself being petulant about it, snapping at Talon when he splashed lake water near her sketchbook, and then apologizing in a mutter while he looked at her like she'd grown a second head. She took her lunch to the far end of the dock and ate it slowly, letting the fact settle instead of fighting it.

That afternoon, Ms. Kerr, the ceramics teacher who came up from the town on Thursdays, was unloading the kiln in the shed behind the cabin. Peyton watched her lift the finished bowls with tongs, each one wrapped in newspaper, and set them on the shelf like sleeping animals. Ms. Kerr did not ask why Peyton was there. She let her watch, and after a while Peyton found she was able to say it out loud.

"I had it all figured out. Ten pieces, one idea. Now I find out the whole thing is bigger than I built it for."

Ms. Kerr set down a bowl with a hairline crack running through its glaze, a piece she did not discard but placed apart from the others, on its own corner of the shelf. "That one opened in the fire," she said. "I like it better now." She peeled off her gloves. "When I was your age I thought a plan was a kind of promise. It's not. It's a first draft of a promise." Then she went back to the kiln, because she was the kind of adult who knew when to stop talking.

Peyton walked back along the shoreline, past the canoe rack, past Talon's shouting paddlers, and turned the problem over the way she turned a pencil in her hand. One way of thinking said the plan was sacred: ten pieces chosen with intention, each one necessary, nothing padded. Another way said the theme itself was the real thing, and the theme was not finished; the empty houses she drew were about absence, and absence kept generating more rooms the longer she looked. She had been treating the number as the frame. Maybe the investigation was the frame, and the number was just the door you walked through.

She also had to admit, standing on the dock while the sun went copper over the water, that she did not know yet whether the five new pieces would deepen the work or dilute it. That part stayed uncertain, and she let it stay. Entropy was the word that came to her from physics class, the way things drift toward disorder unless you keep feeding energy in. Maybe that was what a portfolio was: not a finished house but a decision to keep paying the energy, image after image, until the disorder agreed to mean something.

She sat down on the dock with her sketchbook and started a list, not of drawings but of questions she hadn't asked yet about the houses. What was behind the wallpaper. Who had left the porch swing. What the rooms looked like at night. Beside the list she wrote, in small letters, fifteen, and underlined nothing.

Kayden found her there at dusk with two cups of cocoa from the mess hall. She sat down, looked at the sketchbook open on Peyton's knees, and read the questions without asking permission, which was the kind of friend Kayden was.

"So you're doing it," she said.

"I'm doing it." Peyton closed the sketchbook and held it against her chest, the cover still warm from the day. Out on the water, Talon's last canoe was coming in, and the paddlers were singing something off-key. "Hand me the cocoa," she said.

story:
Logan stacked the last crate of tomatoes and checked his phone again. Dana was ten minutes late, which meant he would be alone with Mr. De Vries for ten more minutes, and Mr. De Vries liked to talk.

"You're the one doing that economics thing," Mr. De Vries said, weighing peppers for a woman in a sun hat. "The presentation." He said it the way people said the word homework, kindly but without much hope for it.

"Tuesday," Logan said. "Explaining how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation." He wiped the scale with a cloth. The market smelled of cut cantaloupe and hot plastic tablecloths; somewhere behind them a guitar case lay open with a few coins in it. "I've got the first half down. Rates go up, borrowing costs more, people buy less, prices stop climbing so fast. It's the second half I can't get right."

Mr. De Vries handed the woman her change and watched her walk away before he answered. "And what's the second half?"

"The part nobody puts on the poster." Logan turned a peach that was bruising where it touched the wood. "My grandfather loves telling it, actually. Last Sunday, at his kitchen table, he started on Volcker. Grandpa kept a newspaper clipping from when the rate hikes finally beat inflation, and he called it the cleanest thing the government ever did. And then my uncle put his coffee down and said, easy for you, you weren't in the unemployment line in eighty-two. I hadn't known that. My uncle lost his job that year. He said unemployment went above ten percent during that recession, ten percent, and he made me say the number back to him twice." The kitchen had gone quiet except for the clock over the stove, and his grandfather had looked at the clipping for a long moment before saying that he still thought it had to be done.

Mr. De Vries had stopped wiping the scale. "What did you say to your uncle?"

"That I was sorry. He said don't be sorry, be accurate." Logan could still see his uncle's hands around the mug, the small tremor of it. "That's the second half. Slowing inflation by raising rates usually costs jobs. It's not a footnote. It's the price."

Dana arrived then, ponytail damp, apologizing about a bus. She and Logan were doing the presentation together, and she slid behind the table beside him and started arranging sweet corn the way the market's ordinance required, husks on, stacked no higher than the crate rim. The city had passed it last spring; Mr. De Vries called it the most circumscribed pile of corn in the state. Dana had laughed at that for a full minute the first time she heard it.

"Okay, run it by me," she said. "Mr. De Vries, you be the teacher. Be merciless."

Mr. De Vries folded his arms. "Young man. You tell me the central bank raises rates. Tell me why I should care."

Logan took a breath that smelled like peaches. "When rates go up, loans get expensive, so people and businesses spend less, and when spending slows, prices stop rising so fast. That's how it tames inflation." He picked up a plum and put it back. "But it's not free. Slowing inflation this way usually costs jobs, because when people stop buying, companies cut workers. In the early eighties, when the Fed hiked rates hard to kill inflation, the recession it caused pushed unemployment above ten percent."

Dana was nodding, but Mr. De Vries wasn't. He was looking at the far end of the market, at the honey stall, and his jaw was working.

"You said your uncle," he said finally. "Eighty-two."

"Yeah. Why?"

Mr. De Vries untied his apron, retied it, untied it again. "Because I was there too. Machine shop outside Akron. Fourteen years, and one morning the foreman read a list of names and mine was on it." He set the apron on the crate of tomatoes. "I don't know if it was the rates or just the recession. Nobody ever told me that, and I've had forty years to wonder. That's the honest answer, and you can put that in your presentation if you want. Nobody ever tells you which part of it was you."

Nobody spoke for a moment. A customer came and Dana sold her a bag of green beans, weighing them with a steadiness that seemed, to Logan, like a kind of mercy.

"I keep wanting there to be a right answer," Logan said quietly, when the customer had gone. "Like, the hikes were good, or they were bad. But my grandfather's clipping and my uncle's unemployment line are both true."

"That's not a failure of your research," Mr. De Vries said. "That's the research." He put his apron back on, took a peach from the bruised pile, and handed it to Logan. "On the house. Eat it before it goes deleterious on me."

Dana laughed. Logan bit into the peach, which was sweeter for the bruise, and juice ran down his wrist and he didn't wipe it away.

story:
The dealership smelled like new carpet and lemon polish, and Zachary had spent enough Saturdays behind the buffer to know that the smell was the most expensive thing on the lot. He worked the detailing bay three days a week, minimum wage plus tips whenever a salesman felt generous, and every dollar went into an envelope in his desk drawer at home. Six hundred and forty dollars. Nine months of weekends.

He'd been saving for a car since October, a notion that had transfigured his whole idea of the future: with a car he could take the shift at the grocery store in Fairview that paid three dollars more an hour, could drive himself to the winter tournaments instead of begging rides, could stop being a person whose plans had to be approved by somebody with keys. Then, three weeks ago, Coach had pulled him aside after practice and mentioned the summer showcase in the city, the one scouts attended. Registration was two hundred and fifty dollars, not counting the bus. The deadline was Monday.

Both were impossible together. That was the arithmetic he carried around the lot on Saturday mornings, wiping handprints off hoods, and no amount of hoping made the envelope in his drawer grow.

"Did you hear that thing yesterday?" Draven asked him at lunch in the break room, phone propped against a sugar jar. Draven worked the phones at the front desk and listened to podcasts through one earbud all day. "The British and the French built this airliner, the Concorde, years back. Spent a fortune on it. And by the time they knew there was no economic case left for it, they kept pouring money in anyway. They'd already spent so much that quitting felt like losing everything." He tipped the earbud out. "It's called the Concorde fallacy. Throwing good money after bad because you can't stand walking away."

"That's stupid," Zachary said. "Once you know it's bad, you stop."

"Everybody says that," Draven said, "right up until they're the ones holding the ticket."

Zachary didn't think about it again until Tommy came in at four, morose in a way that had become his weather. Tommy had quit the detailing bay in January for a kitchen job at the steakhouse on Route 9, and he hated it, and he was still there. He sat down across from Zachary, unlaced his boots, and rotated his ankle like it ached, and the boots were the expensive non-slip kind he'd bought before his first shift, ninety dollars of his own money. "You still doing the showcase?" he asked. "My brother said the scouts actually show up to that one."

"I don't know yet. I've got to decide by Monday. What's it to you?"

"Nothing." Tommy relaced the boot, cinched it too tight. "I'm thinking about getting out of the kitchen. Six months of double shifts and I still want to quit every single day."

"So quit."

"I've got ninety dollars in boots, man. Plus the knife set, plus I already did the worst months, the training months. Leaving now means all that was for nothing."

Zachary opened his mouth to say it was already for nothing either way, then heard the shape of the sentence and shut it. He thought of the governments and the airliner, the money they knew was gone and kept spending anyway. He thought of Draven's line about the ticket, and how certain he himself had sounded at lunch, and how cheap certainty was when it wasn't your money in the boots.

It was Mr. Farah who brought things to a point. The sales manager had noticed Zachary lingering by the used lot on his breaks, had noticed which car he lingered by: a silver Civic, high miles, priced at eight hundred and driveable tomorrow. On Saturday, as Zachary was folding the last chamois, Mr. Farah came into the bay with his jacket already on, keys in hand. "I can do seven fifty on the Civic if your father co-signs," he said. "But I need to know tonight, because there's a man coming at ten tomorrow morning who wants it."

Seven hundred and fifty. Zachary had six hundred and forty and a fifty from his grandmother he'd been pretending wasn't there. The numbers fit. The car could be his by tomorrow afternoon, and Monday's deadline would take care of itself, the way impossibilities do.

He stood by the silver Civic while the lot lights buzzed on, moths beginning their slow circles above the sodium glow. He put his hand flat on the hood, still warm from the sun it had been sitting in all day, and it seemed to him that the showcase was a ticket too, one he couldn't appraise the way Mr. Farah could appraise a trade-in. If he passed on the car, he gave up the better job, the rides, the two years of being his own driver, and if he passed on the showcase he might be giving up something he couldn't even name yet, and no one would ever tell him the price of the thing he hadn't bought. That was the part nobody mentioned when they talked about choices, he thought, wiping a last smudge off the windshield with his sleeve. You never got to see what the other one would have become.

He took out his phone and typed a text to Mr. Farah, deleted it, typed it again, and stood there so long the moths had settled and the lot had gone quiet.

"I'll know by nine," he said finally, out loud, to nobody, and pressed send.

story:
Cameron had drawn the graph four times and it was still wrong. Two axes, fish on one, lumber on the other, a curve bowing between them. Mr. Singh had assigned it on Friday: pick two countries, give each a production possibility frontier, then show what trade could do for them. Cameron's trade point sat stubbornly outside his curve, in blank space, like a plane flying past the edge of a map. He pressed the pencil down until the graph paper dimpled.

"You're wrecking that page," his mother said from the doorway. She set a mug of tea on his desk, close enough to reach but far enough from the ink. "Homework or art project?"

"Neither, apparently." He turned the page so she could see the point floating in the white. "The trade point lands out here. That can't be right. A country can't consume more than it can make."

She peered at it, shrugged with real apology, and told him she'd eviscerated her own economics notes years ago, sold the textbook back for eleven dollars. He thanked her for the tea and heard her pause at the top of the stairs, then go down softly, the way she did when she knew he needed quiet more than help.

He texted Marilou, who was better at graphs, and Bria, who was better at arguing. Both said they'd come. While he waited he redrew the curve one more time, slowly, checking each end. Norway, he had decided, could make either forty tons of fish or twenty of lumber if it put everything into one. Canada could make thirty of fish or thirty of lumber. He'd made up the numbers and now he was trapped by them.

Bria arrived first, dropped her bag on his bed, and bent over the desk with her hands on her knees. "This is a travesty of geometry," she said. "Your axes aren't even the same scale." She took the ruler out of his pencil case without asking, which was how they'd been since fourth grade. Marilou came in ten minutes later smelling of rain, shook out her umbrella, and pulled his desk chair around backward so she could straddle it beside them.

"Okay," Marilou said. "So Canada gives up one ton of fish for every ton of lumber it makes. Norway gives up two tons of fish for every ton of lumber. So Norway should do the fish and Canada should do the lumber. That's the whole thing, that's comparative advantage." She tapped the curve. "Norway has the lower opportunity cost in fish. So Norway makes only fish, Canada makes only lumber, and then they trade."

"But look." Cameron plotted the totals, then split them down a plausible deal, and the point for what each country got to consume landed outside its own curve again. He waited for one of them to laugh. Neither did. Bria leaned closer, and he watched her run it the same direction he had, Norway keeping thirty tons of fish and taking nine of lumber, ending up past the line it could never cross alone. "It's not a mistake," she said slowly. "That's the point of the assignment. By specializing and trading, each country ends up consuming a combination of goods that's beyond what it could produce on its own. Like, actually beyond the frontier. Off the graph's map."

"So what do I write, that everyone wins forever?" Cameron heard his own voice go bellicose, a defensive tone he hated in himself, and lowered it. "Sorry. It's just, someone has to lose, right? That's what my uncle says about trade."

Marilou rotated the page, studying the two curves side by side. "Maybe not the way you drew it," she said. "Maybe both get combinations they couldn't reach alone. That's what the math shows here." She hesitated, which was unlike her. "I don't know what it shows in the real world, with real countries. That part we're not going to settle tonight."

"That's honest, at least," Bria said. She slid the ruler back into the pencil case, then took it out again and set it beside the graph, aligned with the trade line, as if to hold it in place. Cameron copied the diagram onto a fresh sheet, careful and slow, and wrote his first sentence underneath. Outside his window the streetlight came on, and his mother called up that there were leftovers if they wanted them. He kept writing while Marilou and Bria argued pleasantly about the uncle, and the point outside the curve stayed exactly where it was, out past the frontier, in the blank space where nothing had been drawn yet.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
story:
Katherine had the display board under one arm and the folder of data in the other, and she had walked to the library because Reagan had texted that she owed Katherine an apology. She did not feel owed anything. She felt like the vinegar had gone warm in her hands, the way it did before something curdled.

The experiment had been simple, which was the problem. She had tested whether seedlings watered with diluted chamomile tea grew taller than seedlings given plain water, and after three weeks the chamomile trays had won by a margin she could see without measuring. She had measured anyway. Eleven millimetres. At the science fair, Keon had looked at her chart for exactly four seconds and asked whether she had repeated it, whether anyone else had repeated it, whether she had considered that her bedroom window faced east and her neighbor's maple had leafed out mid-trial and changed the light. She had not considered the maple. She had wanted to tell him that the maple was not her variable, that her variable was chamomile, that the whole point of controls was to isolate one thing. Instead she had said something short, and Keon had said "whatever" in the tone people use when they mean the opposite, and Reagan had laughed, and now Reagan was texting about apologies.

She found Reagan at the corner table by the periodicals, headphones half off, and set the board down across from her.

"I didn't laugh at you," Reagan said. "I laughed at the way he said repeat it. Like he's the FDA."

"He's not wrong, though." Katherine sat. "That's the part I can't stop thinking about. He's not wrong and it still felt like an attack."

Reagan pulled one headphone free entirely. "So what are you doing here?"

"Looking for why it felt like that. And whether I should redo it."

She left Reagan guarding the board and went into the stacks. The sociology section was two aisles she had never had reason to visit, shelved between psychology and something called methology before the label corrected itself to methodology. She was looking for anything about how science decides things, because the fair judge, a woman with a lanyard and a clipboard, had written one line on her evaluation card: claims are accepted by a community, not by an experiment. Katherine had read it eleven times on the bus and understood it less each time.

The book she pulled was about the sociology of science, and she stood in the aisle reading it the way you drink from a water fountain too long, bent and unwilling to stop. In 1942, she read, the sociologist Robert K. Merton had named a norm of science organized skepticism. The words sat on the page in that order. Claims, he argued, must survive critical scrutiny by the community before they are accepted. She read the sentence twice. Keon's four seconds and his question about the maple had not been cruelty, or not only. They had been the ordinary weather of the whole enterprise, something scientists were inured to the way sailors were inured to cold spray off a fjord, not because it was pleasant but because it was the climate the work happened in.

She carried the book back to the table and read the passage aloud, quietly, her finger under the line.

"Organized skepticism," Reagan said, when Katherine finished. "That's a great name for it. It sounds like a club you get drafted into."

"It kind of is. He wrote it in 1942, and it's a norm, not a law. Nobody forces it. The community just won't accept a claim until enough people have kicked it around, repeated it, tried to break it."

"So Keon was doing sociology at you without knowing it."

"Keon was doing science at me without knowing it." Katherine closed the book. "Which is almost worse, because I can't be angry and correct."

Ms. Demetriou passed with a cart of returns and paused at their table, her eyes going to the seedling chart. "Are you the chamomile girl? I judged near your aisle. Eleven millimeters, was it?"

"Eleven and a half, averaged."

"Are you redoing it?"

"That's the decision." Katherine looked at the board, at her neat bar graphs, which now seemed to her nascent rather than finished, a first word in a conversation she had mistaken for a verdict. "If I redo it, and it holds, it means more. If I redo it and it doesn't, then Keon caught something real. Either way I'd rather know than win."

Ms. Demetriou stacked two books on her cart that had nothing to do with anything and said, "The window in the study room faces north, if that helps," and rolled on.

That was the twist, though Katherine didn't recognize it as one until later: the library had a room for this. She gathered the board, asked Reagan to carry the folder, and went to claim the key. In the north-facing study room she found Keon already sitting there with three trays of soil and a bag of chamomile, headphones on, a ruler laid parallel to a notebook like an instrument waiting for a hand.

He pulled the headphones off. "I started without you. Same seeds. Your watering schedule's on the shared doc." He turned the notebook so she could read the first page, which was blank except for the date and a column headed plain water and a column headed tea. "I figure my window's different. That's the point, right? Different window, different person."

Katherine set her board against the wall, unopened. She pulled out the chair across from him, took the ruler, and drew her own columns beneath his.

"Take the north window," she said, and marked her first seed.
