activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
story:
The playground behind the community center still had its toddler equipment, a plastic slide and a climbing frame shaped like a doomed spaceship, but for three weeks it had belonged to the summer frisbee league, whose members were seventeen and too proud to admit they were practicing on mulch. Chloe sat on top of the spaceship with her cleats dangling, holding the league's phone with the filmed match from Tuesday, because Tuesday was the match she could not stop replaying.

Teagan climbed up beside her, peeling a tangerine. "You've watched that four times. Mr. Goh is going to eulogize the frisbee at this rate. He gave a whole speech about effort at midfield today."

"He wasn't eulogizing anything. He was mad." Chloe tilted the screen. "Watch this part. Third point. Blake's wide open on the right and I don't throw to her, and then watch her face."

Teagan leaned in, squinting. "She looks like a seagull that got its chip stolen. That's just her concentration face."

"No, she goes flat after that. For the whole rest of the game she stops cutting hard. And I said nothing. I just let it sit there like a dead raccoon between us."

Teagan offered a tangerine segment, which Chloe took, because tangerine diplomacy could not be refused. "So say something to her."

"I tried yesterday. I said she should be more aggressive." Chloe pulled her knees up. "She said, and I quote, 'I am aggressive, you just never look at me.' Then she did a fake laugh and left. So now I have two problems instead of one."

Blake arrived at the base of the spaceship with a water bottle she was using as a microphone. "This just in, local girls scheming on a climbing frame, film at eleven."

Chloe looked down at her, and something in her chest performed a slow, unhelpful somersault. Blake was easy to tease and hard to correct, because Blake treated all criticism as either a joke or a declaration of war, with no middle country. Chloe had spent Thursday night reading, of all things, an article her cousin had sent about how workplaces trained their managers to give feedback, because that was the kind of person Chloe was when a friendship had a dead raccoon in it.

She climbed down to the mulch and turned the phone around. "Blake. Do you have two minutes? I filmed the game and I want to show you something, and I want to try saying it a different way than I did before."

Blake's eyebrows went up, but she sat on the bottom rung. "Is this an intervention? Is Teagan here to hold me down?"

"Teagan is here to eat tangerines and judge us," Chloe said. "Okay. I read this thing. It's a model from the Center for Creative Leadership called Situation-Behavior-Impact. You name when it happened, what the person did, and what effect it had. That's the whole thing. So instead of 'be more aggressive,' which means nothing and also sounds like an insult, I'm going to try the actual version."

Blake made a gesture of go on, but she had gone still in a way that was not unfriendly.

"Tuesday, third point, I had the disc and a look at the right side." Chloe held up one finger, then two. "You made three hard cuts toward the end zone, and each time you slowed down before I even started my windup, like you'd decided in advance I wouldn't throw. And the impact was that I stopped reading you as an option, and we lost the point, and honestly I felt like you didn't trust me, which made me play worse too." She heard her own voice shake slightly on the last clause and kept going anyway. "That's it. That's the whole thing."

Blake peeled the label off her water bottle in one long strip, which was what she did when she was actually thinking. "You counted my cuts?"

"I watched it four times."

"You watched it four times." Blake looked at the label, then at Chloe, then at the doomed spaceship as if it might offer a postulate superior to anything available on the ground. "Okay. Here's mine, then, same rules. Tuesday, fourth point, you had the disc, I was open for two full seconds, and you threw a hospital pass straight to the other team. Impact: I yelled 'CHLOE,' in a tone my grandmother would call unbecoming, and then I sulked for six points because I decided you were being malevolent, which, for the record, I no longer postulate. You were probably just scared of the wind."

"I was scared of the wind," Chloe admitted. "It was a very windy day."

"It's an outdoor league, Chloe."

"I'm aware it's an outdoor league."

Teagan dropped tangerine peel onto both their heads from above, and Blake scrambled up the frame after her, and the three of them ended up in a mulch-scuffling heap by the slide, which was not in any feedback model Chloe had read. Later, when the others had gone for slushies and Chloe was coiling the cones, she turned the thing over once more. She still did not know whether the model would hold on a day when the criticism was bigger than a frisbee throw, or whether naming an impact honestly was kindness or just a tidier way to wound someone. She only knew that Blake had stayed for the whole conversation, and that Thursday's rematch was supposed to be windy again.

She picked up the last cone and, at the edge of the field, heard Blake calling her name from the slushie line, holding up a cup the color of something radioactive.

story:
Alexis had arranged the living room with the seriousness of a stage manager: chips in the auxiliary bowl, the good one reserved for later, chairs angled toward the screen, the good lamp turned off because Dylan insisted it created a glare. By the time the tip-off came, his father had claimed the armchair, Dylan was folded onto the rug, and Marie-Soleil sat on the arm of the couch with her phone face-down on her knee, a gesture of discipline she would not keep for long.

In the third quarter, the Raptors' shooting guard made his fifth consecutive basket, and Dylan rose from the rug like a man witnessing something religious. "He's on fire," Dylan said. "Feed him the ball every possession. He cannot miss tonight."

"Every possession," Alexis's father said, "is exactly how you lose a lead. He's due to miss."

Alexis felt the old argument unfold with the familiarity of furniture. One side believed in the fire, the other in the correction, and neither side ever conceded anything, which was maybe why they enjoyed it. Tonight, though, he wondered whether there was anything underneath the argument besides preference. Was a streak a real thing a player entered, like weather, or just a story people told about randomness after the fact? He took out his phone.

"He's heating up again," Marie-Soleil said, and indeed the guard had made two more, one of them from distance with a hand in his face. She turned her phone over and started typing, which meant she was having the same question, or betting on something, or telling her brother to turn the game on.

Alexis found it quickly, because the internet had already had this argument thousands of times. A study from 1985 by Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky had looked at streak shooting and called the "hot hand" an illusion. That was the phrase the paper used, the exact word, and Dylan would not like it. The study had said, in essence, that what fans saw as fire was just the ordinary wobbling of chance, that a player's makes after makes were no more likely than his makes after misses. For thirty years that had been the settled answer, the one his father would have cited if his father cited anything.

Then, in 2018, two researchers named Miller and Sanjurjo went back over the old study and found a statistical flaw in how the streaks had been counted. When they corrected it, the evidence pointed the other way: streak shooting looked real. Alexis read the sentence twice, partly because he wanted it to be true and partly because he had learned to distrust that wanting. He liked the idea of fire, the idea that a person could catch something and carry it for a while, but liking an idea was not a reason.

"Alexis," his mother called from the kitchen, "the extra dip is in the fridge if you want it." He got up, carried out the small auxiliary errand, and came back to find the argument in full bloom. Dylan was enunciating each word with the exaggerated patience of someone who thought he was surrounded by fools: "You. Give. Him. The. Ball." Marie-Soleil was scrolling with her thumb and holding the phone so her eyes could do two things at once.

"I found something," Alexis said, and the room half-turned, the way a room does when the game goes to a timeout. "There was a study in 1985, Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky. They said the hot hand is an illusion. Streaks aren't real, just chance."

"See," his father said, gesturing with a chip.

"Wait," Alexis said. "In 2018, Miller and Sanjurjo redid it and found a flaw in the statistics. With that fixed, they found evidence of streak shooting." He heard his own voice get quicker, the way it did in seminar when a paper actually worked. "So the fire might be real. Or might not be, exactly. Two smart papers, thirty years apart, opposite answers."

Marie-Soleil had stopped scrolling. "So nobody knows?"

"Two groups of people with numbers think they know," Alexis said. "That might be different."

Dylan pointed at the screen, where the guard was standing in the corner waiting for the inbounds pass, sweat-dark, jaw set, five for five in the quarter or six, nobody in the room quite sure. "Tell your studies he doesn't exist," Dylan said. "Look at him."

Alexis looked. The guard caught the ball, dribbled once without looking down, and rose into his shot with the unhurried certainty of a man closing a door behind him. The whole room leaned forward, Alexis included, papers and flaws and thirty years of argument suspended somewhere above the couch.

It rattled once on the rim, soft, and dropped through.

story:
Eli had parallel parked the family sedan between two recycling bins eleven times in the school parking lot, and on the twelfth attempt he clipped the one standing in for the front bumper. Ms. Romano, his neighbour three doors down, who had agreed to supervise his practice hours in exchange for his hauling her yard waste to the depot in June, watched from the curb with her thermos. She was a taciturn woman who graded his driving the way she graded everything, with a small nod or its absence. Today she gave the nod anyway, which he understood to mean the bins were not people and the sedan was not her car.

The problem was Saturday. Alec had tickets to a show two towns over, no transit after ten, and a mother who had announced she was done being a taxi service for boys old enough to vote. If Eli did not pass the road test on Friday afternoon, Alec's forty dollars would evaporate, and Alec had mentioned this, by Eli's count, every day since Sunday. Alec's older cousin had agreed to be backup driver, but the cousin worked Fridays and Saturdays and, in Alec's phrasing, "smelled like a bait shop," so this was less a plan than a threat.

"You're amortizing the lesson cost over my gratitude," Alec said on Wednesday, riding shotgun while Eli circled the school block for the fourth time. "Every hour you practise, the concert gets more likely. That's basic finance."

"That's not what amortize means."

"It's close enough."

Ms. Romano sat in the back out of some private principle, leaving the front to Alec, who narrated. Eli worked the wheel between the bins until the parking no longer required thought, until his hands did it and the rest of him was free to worry about the other thing, the on-ramp, which no amount of bins could simulate.

The other thing had a history. On Monday, at the ramp onto Route 9, Eli had frozen. He'd crept up the merging lane at forty while the traffic streamed past at highway speed, and a truck had braked behind him, and Ms. Romano had said, quietly, "Again tomorrow," which from her was a paragraph. He'd read the handbook that night under his blanket like contraband. The acceleration lane, it said, was for reaching a speed close to that of highway traffic before merging. Merging slowly, it said, forces others to brake. He had read it four times and still felt the two facts pulling against each other, because everything his body wanted at forty was to slow down, and everything the page wanted was for him to speed up.

Thursday after last period, he drove Alec and Channing, who had attached herself to the operation because her own test was next month and she claimed to learn by osmosis, out to Route 9. In biology they'd just finished a unit on homeostasis, how a system fights to hold its balance, and Channing kept using the word for everything, including the thermostat in the gym and Alec's mood. "This ramp is your homeostasis," she said from the back. "Highway's in equilibrium. You have to arrive already matching it, or you knock the whole thing out."

"That's actually not terrible," Alec said.

Eli signalled, checked the mirror, and entered the acceleration lane with his foot already moving. He brought the car up to a speed close to that of the highway traffic, closer than he had ever voluntarily gone, and looked over his shoulder into a gap that three seconds earlier had been a wall of metal and was now an open doorway. He merged. Nobody braked. The car settled into the lane as though it had always been there, and behind him Channing let out a breath she had apparently been holding since the school lot.

"There's the difference," Alec said. "Monday you made that truck slow down. Now nothing had to change for you."

"It felt like the wrong thing," Eli said. "Going fast to be safe. It still feels backwards."

"Physics doesn't care about your feelings," Channing said, and then, "I'm stealing the homeostasis line for my test."

They took the next exit and looped back so Eli could do it twice more, and both times the gap appeared, or he made it appear, which was possibly the same thing and possibly not, and he could not have said which. On the third pass Ms. Romano, from the back seat where she had sat saying nothing, leaned forward slightly.

"Tomorrow," she said, "the parallel parking comes first. Do it the way you do the bins."

The test was Friday at two. Alec waited in the parking lot with the tickets in his jacket, standing where the bins had stood, arms out like a man measuring a space that wasn't there yet.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
story:
Maelle had read the thermometer wrong the first time, and the chocolate had seized into a grainy gray slab, so on the second evening at the campsite she set the pot in the coals at the edge of the fire and watched the numbers like a hawk. She had brought the couverture in a cooler from home, two kilos of it, because the farmers' market on Saturday had a table for students and she intended to sell dipped apricots and small bark shards, and she refused to sell anything that bent instead of snapping.

Aiyana sat on an overturned crate beside her, sorting apricots by size. "You know it's chocolate," she said. "People will buy it either way."

"They'll buy it once," Maelle said. "Then they'll remember me as the girl with the waxy chocolate."

Jai came back from the washhouse with wet hands and a theory he'd been carrying since lunch, which was that Maelle was pathologizing a batch of candy. She let him have the joke. He was the one who had wandered past Mr. Francis's site that afternoon, and Mr. Francis, who kept an apiary and sold honey at the same market, had mentioned something offhand that Jai now delivered like a dispatch: that the chocolate on the market tables last summer had sat all day in the sun, solid on the table, and still melted the instant you put it in your mouth. Body temperature, he'd said. That was the whole trick. Chocolate set solid below the body and gave up above it.

Maelle stirred and thought about that. She had learned tempering as a procedure, cool it, seed it, warm it back, hold it steady, but she had never thought about what the procedure was for. The chocolate on the table could survive the sun because the crystals that mattered melted at about 33.8 degrees Celsius, a shade under body temperature, and that was why a properly tempered piece held its shape in a warm hand and still dissolved on the tongue. She said it out loud once, without the numbers, and Aiyana frowned and asked how a person could make something sit right on the edge like that, and Maelle said that was exactly what tempering was, as far as she could tell: persuading the fat into the one crystal form out of several that set shiny and snapped clean. She didn't say Form V, because she wasn't sure enough yet to name it. Later she would check her notes against the phone in the car, and the name would be there, and she would feel the small seismic shift of a procedure turning into an understanding, but that came after.

What she had instead was the thermometer reading 45 and falling, and the seed chocolate she'd chopped going in a handful at a time, and the shine beginning to come up on the surface like a steppe horizon at the end of rain, wide and level and sudden. Jai leaned over the pot with the flashlight. The marsh behind them was ticking with frogs. Somewhere down the loop a child was being called to bed in a patient, practiced voice.

"Test it," Aiyana said.

Maelle dipped the tip of a knife and laid the smear on a strip of foil on the cool stone table. They all watched it as though it might do something theatrical. It did nothing. It sat. Then, after a minute that felt longer, it dulled slightly and set with a dry edge, and when she pressed her fingernail to it, it resisted and then gave with a faint click.

"That's it," she said, though she kept the doubt in her voice on purpose, because a smear was not a shard and a cool stone was not a July table in direct sun.

They dipped apricots until the light failed, working fast, and set the tray inside the car with the windows cracked, which was a compromise between humidity and raccoons that Maelle was not entirely satisfied with. In the morning the chocolate had held its gloss, and she broke a corner off a shard and it snapped, cleanly, the sound more like a twig than a candy, and the broken face was matte and tight and looked like slate.

Aiyana put a piece in her mouth and closed her eyes. "It's gone already," she said. "It wasn't like that yesterday."

At the market, Mr. Francis came by near noon, when the sun was flat on the table and the samples had sat out for two hours without a bloom mark. He picked up a shard, held it in his closed fist for a slow count, then ate it. Maelle watched him, wanting the verdict and also not wanting it, because his fist was one test and a customer's mouth was another and she was beginning to suspect that the space between them, that degree and a half or so, was the whole art and not something she would ever fully own. He turned the remaining piece over in his fingers, unmarked by his hand.

"Solid in the fist," he said, "and it vanished the moment it touched my tongue. You held it right on the line."

Maelle looked at the tray, at the shine she could see her own face in, and reached for another apricot. "The next batch is on the table in ten minutes," she said.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
story:
The playground behind the middle school had one piece of equipment Anthony still visited: a rusted basketball hoop with no net, its backboard warped by some long-ago winter. He stood at the free-throw line with Siena's borrowed physics worksheet folded in his back pocket and a tennis ball in his hand, because the quiz was Monday and the problems might as well have been written in Sumerian.

"Mr. Wang says you split the velocity," Siena had told him on Friday, leaning across the aisle, her pencil tapping the diagram of a cannon on a cliff. "Horizontal and vertical. They don't talk to each other." Anthony had nodded the way he nodded in class, which was to externalize an understanding he did not have, a performance for the teacher's benefit and his own. He'd copied the equations. He'd copied the arrows. Nothing had stuck.

That was the night he remembered now, standing at the line in the cold. His father had been in the kitchen, and Anthony had taken a ball out to the driveway to time a throw with his phone, mostly to avoid the kitchen. His father had come to the doorway with a dish towel over his shoulder and watched without comment, and the silence between them had felt like a held breath. Anthony had thrown the ball straight up, caught it, thrown it again, and on the third throw he'd actually watched the numbers. The ball had left his hand fast. It had slowed, hung, fallen. He'd expected the fall to take longer than the rise, some instinct telling him that climbing is harder than descending. The timer said otherwise. Up and down had matched.

"Nine point eight," Siena said now, arriving with her bike, one wheel still spinning as she dropped it in the wood chips. "Metres per second. Every second." She held out her hand for the ball. "Vertical only. Mr. Wang said it twice and you were drawing that shark."

"I wasn't drawing a shark."

"You were drawing a shark."

He threw her the ball underhand, a lazy lob, and she caught it and launched it high over the hoop, higher than necessary, and they both watched it hang. "Same rate up as down," she said. "Whether it's rising or falling. Nine point eight each second." Then she looked at him sideways. "You didn't come to Oceanne's thing last night."

"I had this."

"Nobody has a worksheet on a Saturday."

He picked up a wood chip and split it with his thumbnail. Oceanne's thing had been a goodbye, he suspected, though nobody had said so. Her family was moving in March and she'd invited everyone from chemistry, and Anthony had chosen rust and numbers instead, and he hadn't decided yet whether that was cowardice or honesty. He suspected his father, also leaving, though nobody had said that either. The dish towel. The doorway. The not-commenting.

"Throw it at the hoop," Siena said. "But tell me where you're aiming before you do."

"Top of the square."

"That's your vertical. The distance is your horizontal. Time connects them. That's the whole quiz." She bounced the ball once, hard, and the sound cracked across the empty playground. "Go on. Aim wrong on purpose."

He aimed at the top of the square, which he would normally have done anyway, and the ball clanked off the front rim. He did it again, aiming higher than felt reasonable, and the ball dropped through the netless hoop, clean, nothing but a soft thud on the asphalt. Siena said nothing, which was louder than saying something. He retrieved the ball and stood there holding it, running the numbers in his head, the rising and the falling at the same relentless rate, the horizontal stroll of the ball across the sky, undisturbed, going its own way while everything vertical fought and surrendered.

"Here's the thing," he said. "I can do the problems now. I think I actually can. But I don't get why it's the same going up as coming down. Nobody's told me that and the book doesn't."

Siena shrugged. "Mr. Wang says that's next semester."

"Next semester," Anthony said. He looked past her at the hoop, at the square he'd aimed at, at the invisible arc he could now calculate but not quite believe in. "Everything important is next semester."

Siena held out her hand for the ball again. "Oceanne's still awake, probably. Her mom lets her have people over till eleven."

Anthony weighed the ball in his palm, its fuzz worn to shine on one side, the lineage of a hundred other hands on it, his father's probably, years ago, in this same yard. The putative excuse of the worksheet sat folded in his pocket, still available, still believable.

"Give me one more shot," he said. "Then we go."

He stepped to the line, aimed above what felt right, and let it go.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
story:
My grandfather says I have been practicing the blessing in the car for two weeks, which is a lie, because it has been nine days, and two of those days I was only mumbling. My mother says I have nothing to be nervous about, which is also a lie, because if I had nothing to be nervous about, my hands would not be sweating through my shirt cuffs on the drive to Aunt Rina's house. "You're going to be great," Jaxson said from the passenger seat, holding my phone with the recording of Grandpa's voice. "Although honestly, man, you've played this thing so many times I could say it myself." Colton, from the back, cleared his throat and recited the first four words with a truly offensive accent, and I told him that if he butchered it at the table tonight, my grandmother would never forgive him, which was not a lie at all.

Here is the situation, as I understand it. Kiddush is a blessing recited over wine or grape juice to begin Sabbath and Jewish festival meals, marking the day as holy. Grandpa has said it at every holiday table since before I was born, and this year, because his voice is going and because I am seventeen and apparently it is time, he asked me. He asked me in the kitchen in October, while washing his hands, without looking up, which is how he asks for things that matter. I said yes before I understood what I was agreeing to, which is a habit of mine.

The problem, which I discovered around day three of car practice, is that there are two ways to do this, and each person who cared enough to weigh in cared very loudly. Grandpa sings it, slow and ornamented, the tune his own father used, and when he finishes, the room hums like something struck. My cousin Danit's husband, who converted a few years ago and is more precise about ritual than anyone born into it, says it plainly, each word clean, because in his community the melody is a distraction from the meaning. "The words are the thing," he told me at Rosh Hashanah, tapping the table. "Sing them if you must, but know them first."

I had privately decided that the husband was wrong and Grandpa was right, because Grandpa is Grandpa. Then I spent an afternoon with my phone, listening to recordings from a synagogue I found online, and something shifted. The plain version, word by word, did something to me I did not expect. It slowed the meaning down until I could hear it: the blessing over the fruit of the vine, the blessing that sets the day apart. I had been singing sounds for years without ever once hearing sentences. But then I would put on Grandpa's recording and feel that other thing too, the way the tune carries the room, the way my grandmother closes her eyes at the same note every single time, like a boat finding a channel.

"Are you having a crisis?" Jaxson asked when I played him both versions in the parking lot before tonight's dinner. "Because this feels like a crisis."

"It's a synthesis," I said.

"You don't know what that word means."

"I looked it up."

I had, in fact, looked it up, and also read half of a philosophy forum thread at two in the morning, which either invigorated my thinking or ruined my sleep, possibly both. Somewhere in there I stopped trying to decide which way was correct and started thinking about what the blessing is actually for. It marks the day as holy. That is its whole job, whether it arrives on a melody or on plain words, and maybe the argument between Grandpa and the husband is less like a fight over right and wrong and more like two people building the same door out of different wood. I could not fully convince myself of this. Part of me still believes the tune is the door, and part of me still believes the words are, and I decided, somewhere between the parking lot and Aunt Rina's front steps, to hold both and stop pretending I had settled it.

Mr. Adeyemi from next door was already at the table when we came in, because Aunt Rina invites him every year and every year he brings his own bottle of sparkling juice and asks, with total seriousness, whether this is the one where he gets to hide the bread. "Different holiday," I told him, and he said, "They can't all have hiding, I suppose," with such sullen disappointment that my grandmother laughed into her napkin. He leaned over as I sat down. "So you're the one tonight. My grandmother made me lead the toast at every gathering from age twelve. My hands shook until I was twenty." He held his up, perfectly steady. "Then they shook again when she died. Different kind of shaking." He patted my wrist and turned back to his glass, and I did not know what to do with that, so I did nothing.

The table filled. My grandmother poured the wine and the grape juice, juice for the kids and for Mr. Adeyemi, who was driving. Grandpa sat at his place but the cup came to me, and everyone went quiet in that way that is somehow loud. I stood up. My prepared remarks, which I had rehearsed, evaporated. I looked at Grandpa, and I looked at the husband, and then I looked at the cup, which caught the light from the chandelier like a small bright lake, and I opened my mouth.

I said the words plainly, every one, the way the husband had taught the internet to teach me, clean and unhurried, and then, at the line where Grandpa's melody always lifts off the ground, I let it lift. Not the whole tune. Just enough of it that my grandmother's eyes closed at the right note, and Grandpa looked up at me with an expression I had never seen before and could not read at all.

"Well," Mr. Adeyemi said, raising his sparkling juice. "To the shakers."

"To the shakers," said Grandpa, and reached for the bread.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
story:
Connor had wanted to act in the spring one-acts, and when the cast list went up without his name on it, Mr. Nikolaidis called him aside in the hallway by the theatre doors and asked him to direct instead. He said it the way he said most things, briefly, already turning away, and Connor agreed before he had decided to. That was in March. By the second week of April he had learned that directing was mostly standing in the dark rows of the house while other people stood in the light, and asking them to move two steps to the left.

The play was a short one about two sisters arguing over a phone call neither of them had made. Salma played the older sister and she was voluble in rehearsal, generous with ideas, offering interpretations of her character that arrived faster than Connor could answer them. The other actor was quieter, a boy from his chemistry class who kept his hands in his pockets even when the script demanded otherwise. Between them, Connor tried to titrate his corrections the way he titrated acid into base in the lab, one drop at a time, watching for the moment the colour changed. Too much at once and Salma would defend herself for ten minutes; too little and the scene stayed flat.

Samira was the stage manager. She sat at a folding table just offstage with a thick binder, and at first Connor paid her no attention, assuming she was there for props and attendance. Then one afternoon he watched her work. Every time he set a movement, her pencil moved. "That's your cross," she said once, when Salma asked why she had to do it again. "Downstage left, three steps, then turn." She tapped the page, where a tiny diagram of the stage was marked with arrows and abbreviations. "It's in the prompt book now."

Connor leaned over the binder during a break. The pages were dense, not just with movements but with pauses, entrances, where the chair went, when the lamp switched on. He asked how she remembered all of it. "I don't remember it," she said. "I wrote it down." She said it plainly, the way you'd say water is wet, and he felt slightly foolish, as though he'd been carrying something heavy that had a handle he'd never noticed.

Still, he distrusted it a little. The arrows on the page were fixed and the actors were not. On the Thursday before opening, Salma decided her big monologue worked better delivered from the window instead of the table, and she was probably right, it was warmer there, more human, and Connor let it stand. He didn't tell Samira. He told himself the moment was alive and the page was not, and that a living thing beat a written one. Mr. Nikolaidis, passing through the theatre on his way out, said only, "You're the director. It's your call." He meant it as permission, but Connor heard the other half of it too.

Opening night, the little theatre was fuller than he expected. The first scene went well. Then, in the monologue, Salma walked to the table. Not the window. She was tired, or the nerves had pulled her back to the safe road, and she delivered the speech beautifully from a place he had stopped believing in. The monologue landed anyway, the audience leaned in, and after the curtain call Salma found him in the lobby, glowing, and asked how it went. "You were at the table," he said. She frowned. "Was I? I thought the window." They stood there a moment while the lobby emptied, and then Connor said, "Which do you want?"

In the green room after, Samira had the binder open. "The window's crossed out," she said, running her finger down the page. "Thursday's note. It says you approved the change and I never got it, so the book still has the table." That was the whole of it, laid out in pencil. The prompt book held the record so that the blocking could be repeated the same way at every performance, and the book said table, and Salma had done table, and there had been no argument to have. Connor realized he wasn't sure whether the record had saved them or merely settled a question that the performance itself had already answered differently.

He sat down next to Samira and took the pencil. There were two more performances. He drew a small arrow through the crossed-out note, then hesitated, because he honestly did not know which version he believed in, the one he had chosen or the one that had happened without him. He looked at Salma, who was pulling bobby pins from her hair, and then at the stage beyond the half-open door, still lit, the chair exactly where the diagram said it should be. Samira slid the binder closer and waited, pencil sharp, the page blank under the lamp.

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
story:
The cuff hissed, beeped, and printed its verdict on the little screen: 142 over 88. Eva read it twice, then looked at her mother, who was peeling an orange at the counter as though the machine were merely a rude guest.

"That's not right," Eva said. "The bottom number's under 90. That's fine, isn't it?"

"The nurse didn't think so." Her mother separated another segment and offered it across the kitchen island, which was her way of changing the subject while appearing generous. "She said stage 2. Stage 2, Eva. It sounds like a play I would fall asleep in."

Eva took the orange segment anyway. She had a want now, sharp and specific: she wanted to understand what the machine had accused her mother of, because the accusation had landed on her too, the way family diagnoses always landed sideways. She carried the pamphlet from the doctor's office to the kitchen table, where Kacey was already sitting, ostensibly to help her study for the nursing assistant course they were both starting in the fall, actually to eat the orange.

"Look at this." Eva pushed the pamphlet across. The table was still sticky from that morning's maple syrup, an atavistic residue of the pancake era their household had supposedly outgrown, and the paper stuck, then released with a small kiss.

Kacey read with her mouth full. "Stage 2 hypertension means systolic 140 or higher, or diastolic 90 or higher."

"Or. It's or, not and." Eva sat back, feeling the click of it. "So 142 over 88. The bottom's under 90, but the top's over 140, and either one is enough. That's why the nurse said it. Either one. It's like a club with two doors."

"A very bad club," Kacey said. "The sort of club where the bouncer is a cardiologist."

Their neighbor Ms. Li knocked then, returning Eva's mother's measuring cups, which she had expropriated three weeks earlier for a batch of mooncakes and defended ever since with polite, immovable excuses. She set them by the sink, noticed the monitor on the counter, and raised an eyebrow at it.

"The machine has opinions," Eva's mother said.

"Are they going to take the good soy sauce next?" Ms. Li asked. "When they've finished with the salt?" But she said it lightly, and she sat down at the table without being asked, which meant she intended to stay for the interesting part.

Eva turned the pamphlet toward her. "Is this right? Either number high enough counts, even if the other one's fine?"

Ms. Li nodded once, unsurprised, and stole a piece of orange, which Kacey defended with a fork. Nobody explained further, because there was nothing further to explain; Eva had already worked it out herself, and that, she was discovering, was the whole difference between memorizing something and owning it.

"So what changes it?" she asked. "The pamphlet keeps saying diet and exercise, but it doesn't say how, exactly. It's like a recipe that says serves four."

"Then cook it and see," Ms. Li said. "That is what the recipe is for."

The next two weeks became a kitchen experiment with a sample size of one, which Kacey insisted on calling "a monomer study," because she had learned the word in chemistry and refused to let it go to waste. Eva rebuilt the grocery list around it: less of the instant noodles that had quietly colonized the top shelf, more of the vegetables Ms. Li brought over in exchange for continued access to the soy sauce. Her mother began walking the loop around the park with Ms. Li in the evenings, the two of them complaining about each other's pace in a way that was, Eva suspected, the actual point of the walks.

Every few days they took the reading together. 138 over 84. Then 135 over 82. Eva logged the numbers in a spiral notebook, drew a graph, and resisted the urge to draw conclusions from a line this short, this noisy, this full of evenings when her mother had walked and evenings when she had watched television instead. The trend was probably real. She could not prove it was, and she said so at dinner, which Kacey found hilarious.

"You're the only person who makes a success story sound like an apology."

"It's not a story yet," Eva said. "It's four data points and a wish."

The morning before her mother's follow-up appointment, they took one more reading in the kitchen, the cuff hissing its familiar breath over the same spot on the same arm, her mother holding still this time instead of arguing with the machine while it worked. The number came up on the screen and Eva copied it down, then sat looking at it while the orange sat unpeeled between them.

"Tell me the number," her mother said.

"I'll tell you after the doctor does," Eva said, and closed the notebook, and slid it across the sticky table toward her.
